title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-4:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var} + \text{Bias}^2\)
MVUE: Unbiased estimator with minimum variance
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
MLE and MME: Systematic methods for constructing estimators


Today’s Goals:

Understand sufficient statistics: data reduction without information loss
Learn the Neyman Factorization Theorem
Connect sufficiency to finding MVUEs via Rao-Blackwell
Define completeness and its role in optimal estimation

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Motivating Question: Data Reduction
Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?







The Key Insight


If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).





Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Mean?
Imagine you’re a consulting statistician. A colleague ran an experiment and wants your help estimating \(\theta\).
Scenario 1: They give you all raw data: \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 3\)
Scenario 2: They only tell you the total: \(T = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4\)

Question: Does Scenario 1 give you more information about \(\theta\) than Scenario 2?


If the answer is no—if knowing \(T\) tells you everything about \(\theta\)—then \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Defects (Devore 7.25)
Setup: The number of major defects on new vehicles follows \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(n = 3\) vehicles with defects \(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0, X_3 = 3\).
Key Question: Would knowing only \(T = \sum X_i = 4\) provide the same information about \(\mu\) as knowing all individual \(X_i\)’s?

Consider: Given that \(T = 4\), what’s the conditional probability of \((X_1, X_2, X_3) = (2, 1, 1)\)?
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!}}{\frac{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4}{4!}} = \frac{4}{27}\]








Critical Observation


The \(\mu\) terms cancel out! The conditional probability doesn’t depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T = t\) does not depend on \(\theta\), for every possible value \(t\).




In other words: Once you know the value of \(T\), the distribution of the data no longer involves \(\theta\)—so no additional information about \(\theta\) can be extracted.








Intuition


\(T\) is sufficient if it “captures” all the information in the data relevant to \(\theta\). It’s sufficient to know \(T\); the raw data adds nothing more.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Factorization Theorem
text:
Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Factorization Theorem
Computing conditional distributions is difficult. The Neyman Factorization Theorem provides an elegant shortcut.






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)


Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta)\) denote the joint pmf or pdf. Then \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if and only if:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) depends on the data only through \(T\) and involves \(\theta\)
\(h\) depends on the data but not on \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Understanding the Factorization
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \underbrace{g(T; \theta)}_{\text{Involves } \theta \text{ and data through } T} \cdot \underbrace{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}_{\text{Depends on data, not } \theta}\]







Strategy for Finding Sufficient Statistics



Write down the joint pmf/pdf
Identify the part that involves \(\theta\)
Factor it so \(\theta\) appears only with a function of the data
That function is your sufficient statistic!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 1: Poisson Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^t}_{g(t; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 2: Uniform Distribution (Devore 7.27)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta) \cdot I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(t; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]








Result


\(T = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).
Note: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient here!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?

# Two samples with same mean but different maxima
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)  # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10) # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 



These have the same \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)

Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses information about \(\theta\)!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Jointly Sufficient Statistics
When there are multiple parameters, we need multiple sufficient statistics.

Example: Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both unknown:
\[f = \frac{1}{\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}\]








Result


\((\bar{X}, S^2)\) or equivalently \((\sum X_i, \sum X_i^2)\) are jointly sufficient for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Minimal Sufficient Statistics
Sufficient statistics are not unique! The entire dataset is always (trivially) sufficient.







Definition


A sufficient statistic \(T\) is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic.





Intuition: Minimal sufficient statistics achieve the greatest data reduction without losing information.








Practical Criterion (Devore 7.74)


\(T\) is minimal sufficient if the likelihood ratio \(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta)/f(\mathbf{y}; \theta)\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\) if and only if \(t(\mathbf{x}) = t(\mathbf{y})\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters for Estimation
Key Question: How do we use sufficient statistics to find better estimators?







Rao-Blackwell Theorem


If \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) and \(U\) is any unbiased estimator for \(h(\theta)\), then:
\[U^* = E(U | T)\]
satisfies:

\(U^*\) is unbiased for \(h(\theta)\)
\(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\) (with equality only if \(U\) is already a function of \(T\))






In words: Conditioning on sufficient statistics never increases variance and often decreases it.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Proof of Rao-Blackwell
Step 1: \(U^*\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\) (since \(T\) is sufficient)
Step 2: By Law of Total Expectation: \[E(U^*) = E[E(U|T)] = E(U) = h(\theta) \checkmark\]
Step 3: By Law of Total Variance: \[\text{Var}(U) = \text{Var}(E[U|T]) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)] = \text{Var}(U^*) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)]\]
Since \(E[\text{Var}(U|T)] \geq 0\), we have \(\text{Var}(U) \geq \text{Var}(U^*)\) ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Zero-Defect Probability (Devore 7.30)
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\).
Crude estimator: \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) is unbiased since \(E(U) = P(X_1 = 0) = e^{-\mu}\)

Apply Rao-Blackwell: With sufficient statistic \(T = \sum X_i\):
\[U^* = P(X_1 = 0 | T = t) = \frac{P(X_1 = 0) \cdot P(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i = t)}{P(T = t)} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^t\]








Improved Estimator


\(U^* = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^T\) is unbiased with smaller variance!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Simulation: Rao-Blackwell Improvement


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5; n <- 10; n_sims <- 5000

poisson_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum
  )

poisson_sim |> 
  select(crude_U, improved_U) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Estimator", values_to = "Estimate") |> 
  mutate(Estimator = ifelse(Estimator == "crude_U", "Crude: I(X₁=0)", "Improved: (1-1/n)^T")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Estimate, fill = Estimator)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(-mu_true), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Rao-Blackwell: Variance Reduction Through Sufficiency",
       subtitle = paste0("True e^(-μ) = ", round(exp(-mu_true), 3)), x = "Estimate", y = "Frequency") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "steelblue")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key Implication






Corollary


Any estimator that is not based purely on sufficient statistics is necessarily inferior to some other estimator.




Also: MLEs always depend on data only through sufficient statistics (because maximizing \(L(\theta) = g(T;\theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\) is equivalent to maximizing \(g\)).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Final Piece: Completeness
Question: Given a sufficient statistic \(T\), is there a unique best unbiased estimator based on \(T\)?







Definition: Complete Statistic


A statistic \(T\) is complete if for any function \(g\):
\[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]





Intuition: The only unbiased estimator of zero based on \(T\) is the zero function itself.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem






Theorem (Lehmann-Scheffé)


If \(T\) is a complete sufficient statistic and \(U = h(T)\) is unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(U\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).




Key fact: For exponential family distributions (Normal, Poisson, Exponential, Binomial, Gamma), the natural sufficient statistics are typically complete.








The Power of Completeness + Sufficiency


Once we find a complete sufficient statistic, any unbiased function of it is automatically the MVUE!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Road to MVUE: Summary
Method 1: Via Sufficiency

Find sufficient statistic \(T\) (Factorization Theorem)
Check completeness (exponential family → typically complete)
Find unbiased function of \(T\) → MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)


Method 2: Via Cramér-Rao

Compute Fisher Information \(I(\theta)\)
Find CRLB = \(1/[nI(\theta)]\)
Find estimator achieving CRLB → MVUE

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lesson 5: Key Takeaways
1. Sufficiency: \(T\) captures all information about \(\theta\) in the data
2. Neyman Factorization: \(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\) identifies sufficient statistics
3. Rao-Blackwell: Conditioning on sufficient statistics improves estimators
4. Completeness + Sufficiency → Unique MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

satisfies:

\(U^*\) is unbiased for \(h(\theta)\)
\(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\) (with equality only if \(U\) is already a function of \(T\))






In words: Conditioning on sufficient statistics never increases variance and often decreases it.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Proof of Rao-Blackwell
Step 1: \(U^*\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\) (since \(T\) is sufficient)
Step 2: By Law of Total Expectation: \[E(U^*) = E[E(U|T)] = E(U) = h(\theta) \checkmark\]
Step 3: By Law of Total Variance: \[\text{Var}(U) = \text{Var}(E[U|T]) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)] = \text{Var}(U^*) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)]\]
Since \(E[\text{Var}(U|T)] \geq 0\), we have \(\text{Var}(U) \geq \text{Var}(U^*)\) ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Zero-Defect Probability (Devore 7.30)
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\).
Crude estimator: \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) is unbiased since \(E(U) = P(X_1 = 0) = e^{-\mu}\)

Apply Rao-Blackwell: With sufficient statistic \(T = \sum X_i\):
\[U^* = P(X_1 = 0 | T = t) = \frac{P(X_1 = 0) \cdot P(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i = t)}{P(T = t)} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^t\]








Improved Estimator


\(U^* = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^T\) is unbiased with smaller variance!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Simulation: Rao-Blackwell Improvement


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5; n <- 10; n_sims <- 5000

poisson_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum
  )

poisson_sim |> 
  select(crude_U, improved_U) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Estimator", values_to = "Estimate") |> 
  mutate(Estimator = ifelse(Estimator == "crude_U", "Crude: I(X_1=0)", "Improved: (1-1/n)^T")) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = Estimate, fill = Estimator)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exp(-mu_true), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "Rao-Blackwell: Variance Reduction Through Sufficiency",
       subtitle = paste0("True e^(-μ) = ", round(exp(-mu_true), 3)), x = "Estimate", y = "Frequency") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("orange", "steelblue")) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key Implication






Corollary


Any estimator that is not based purely on sufficient statistics is necessarily inferior to some other estimator.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Do MLEs Use Sufficient Statistics?
Key Question: What is the relationship between MLEs and sufficient statistics?







Theorem: MLEs Are Functions of Sufficient Statistics


If \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\), then the MLE \(\hat{\theta}\) can always be expressed as a function of \(T\) alone.





Proof: By the factorization theorem: \[L(\theta) = f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\]
Maximizing \(L(\theta)\) is equivalent to maximizing \(g(T; \theta)\) since \(h(\mathbf{x})\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\).
Therefore \(\hat{\theta}\) depends on the data only through \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Example: MLE Uses the Sufficient Statistic
text:
Example: MLE Uses the Sufficient Statistic
Poisson\((\mu)\):

Sufficient statistic: \(T = \sum X_i\)
MLE: \(\hat{\mu} = \bar{X} = T/n\) ✓ (function of \(T\))


Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\):

Sufficient statistics: \((\sum X_i, \sum X_i^2)\) or equivalently \((\bar{X}, S^2)\)
MLEs: \(\hat{\mu} = \bar{X}\), \(\hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\) ✓ (functions of sufficient statistics)



Uniform\([0, \theta]\):

Sufficient statistic: \(T = \max(X_i)\)
MLE: \(\hat{\theta} = \max(X_i) = T\) ✓ (is the sufficient statistic itself!)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Are MLEs Themselves Sufficient?
Important distinction:

MLEs are functions of sufficient statistics ✓
But MLEs are not always sufficient themselves ✗








MLEs ≠ Sufficient Statistics


The MLE \(\hat{\theta}\) is sufficient only if \(\hat{\theta}\) and the sufficient statistic \(T\) determine each other (one-to-one correspondence).





Example where MLE IS sufficient:

Uniform\([0, \theta]\): MLE = \(\max(X_i)\) = sufficient statistic ✓

Example where MLE is NOT sufficient:

Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\): MLEs are \((\hat{\mu}, \hat{\sigma}^2)\), which ARE jointly sufficient
But if we only want \(\hat{\mu} = \bar{X}\), this alone is not sufficient for both parameters

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why This Matters






Practical Implications



MLEs are efficient: They automatically use all available information about \(\theta\)
Finding MLEs: Once you identify sufficient statistics, you only need to maximize \(g(T; \theta)\)—often simpler!
Asymptotic optimality: MLEs achieve the Cramér-Rao bound asymptotically, partly because they use sufficient statistics





Bottom line: Sufficiency explains why MLEs have such good properties—they never “waste” information in the data.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Connecting MLE, Sufficiency, and MVUE







MLE is always a function of sufficient statistics
If the sufficient statistic is complete, unbiased functions of it are MVUEs
For large \(n\), MLEs are approximately MVUEs (asymptotic efficiency)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Final Piece: Completeness
Question: Given a sufficient statistic \(T\), is there a unique best unbiased estimator based on \(T\)?







Definition: Complete Statistic


A statistic \(T\) is complete if for any function \(g\):
\[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]





Intuition: The only unbiased estimator of zero based on \(T\) is the zero function itself.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem






Theorem (Lehmann-Scheffé)


If \(T\) is a complete sufficient statistic and \(U = h(T)\) is unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(U\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).




Key fact: For exponential family distributions (Normal, Poisson, Exponential, Binomial, Gamma), the natural sufficient statistics are typically complete.








The Power of Completeness + Sufficiency


Once we find a complete sufficient statistic, any unbiased function of it is automatically the MVUE!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Road to MVUE: Summary
Method 1: Via Sufficiency

Find sufficient statistic \(T\) (Factorization Theorem)
Check completeness (exponential family → typically complete)
Find unbiased function of \(T\) → MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)


Method 2: Via Cramér-Rao

Compute Fisher Information \(I(\theta)\)
Find CRLB = \(1/[nI(\theta)]\)
Find estimator achieving CRLB → MVUE

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lesson 5: Key Takeaways
1. Sufficiency: \(T\) captures all information about \(\theta\) in the data
2. Neyman Factorization: \(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\) identifies sufficient statistics
3. Rao-Blackwell: Conditioning on sufficient statistics improves estimators
4. Completeness + Sufficiency → Unique MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

Welcome to Statistical Inference!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Today’s Goals

Understand the fundamental problem of statistical inference
Distinguish between populations and samples, parameters and statistics
Use R to simulate sampling distributions
Review key properties of expected value and variance

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Motivating Example: Clinical Trial
A pharmaceutical company is testing a new blood pressure medication.
The Question: What is the true average reduction in systolic blood pressure?

What we have: Data from 25 patients in a trial

# Actual blood pressure reductions (mmHg) from 25 patients
bp_reductions <- c(12, 8, 15, 10, 7, 14, 11, 9, 13, 16,
                   8, 12, 10, 14, 11, 9, 15, 13, 7, 12,
                   10, 8, 14, 11, 13)

# What's our estimate of the true mean reduction?
mean(bp_reductions)

[1] 11.28




This “estimate” is the observed value of the (random variable) sample mean statistic: \(\bar{X} = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\)


But how reliable is this estimate? Would we get the same answer with different patients?

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The Big Picture: Population vs Sample
text:
The Big Picture: Population vs Sample


Key insight: We use sample data to make inferences about population parameters.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Key Terminology (Devore 6.1)






Definitions



Population: The entire collection of individuals or measurements of interest
Sample: A subset of the population that we actually observe
Parameter: A numerical characteristic of the population (e.g., \(\mu\), \(\sigma\), \(p\))
Statistic: A numerical characteristic computed from sample data (e.g., \(\bar{X}\), \(S\), \(\hat{p}\))





The Central Challenge: Parameters are fixed but unknown; statistics are known but random.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Parameters vs. Statistics








Concept
Population (Parameter)
Sample (Statistic)




Mean
\(\mu\)
\(\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i\)


Variance
\(\sigma^2\)
\(S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\)


Proportion
\(p\)
\(\hat{p} = X/n\)


Maximum
\(\theta\) (upper bound)
\(\max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\)




Key Point: Parameters use Greek letters; statistics use Roman letters or “hats.”

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Sampling Process (Devore 6.2)
Random Sampling Assumptions:

Each observation \(X_i\) is a random variable
The \(X_i\) are independent of each other
Each \(X_i\) has the same distribution (identically distributed)


Together: \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) are i.i.d. (independent and identically distributed)








Why This Matters


The i.i.d. assumption allows us to derive the properties of statistics mathematically.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Review: Expected Value
The expected value \(E(X)\) is the long-run average of a random variable.






Key Properties We’ll Use Today



\(E(c) = c\) for any constant \(c\)
\(E(cX) = c \cdot E(X)\)
\(E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y)\)
\(E\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) = \sum_{i=1}^n E(X_i)\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Worked Example: Expected Value of Sample Mean
text:
Worked Example: Expected Value of Sample Mean
Problem: If \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) are iid observations from a population with mean \(\mu\), what is \(E(\bar{X})\)?

Solution: Let’s work through this step by step.
\[E(\bar{X}) = E\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)\]


\[= \frac{1}{n} E\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) \quad \text{(Property 2: constants come out)}\]


\[= \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n E(X_i) \quad \text{(Property 4: sum of expectations)}\]


\[= \frac{1}{n} \cdot n\mu = \mu \quad \text{(Each } E(X_i) = \mu \text{)}\]

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Your Turn: Calculate Expected Value
Exercise: A hospital measures the recovery time (in days) for patients after surgery. Let \(X_1, X_2, X_3\) be recovery times for 3 patients. The population mean recovery time is \(\mu = 5\) days.
Questions:

What is \(E(X_1)\)?
What is \(E(X_1 + X_2 + X_3)\)?
What is \(E(\bar{X})\) where \(\bar{X} = \frac{X_1 + X_2 + X_3}{3}\)?


Answers:

\(E(X_1) = \mu = 5\) days
\(E(X_1 + X_2 + X_3) = 5 + 5 + 5 = 15\) days
\(E(\bar{X}) = \frac{15}{3} = 5\) days

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Review: Variance
Variance measures the spread of a distribution: \(\text{Var}(X) = E[(X - \mu)^2]\)






Key Properties We’ll Use Today



\(\text{Var}(c) = 0\) for any constant
\(\text{Var}(cX) = c^2 \cdot \text{Var}(X)\)
If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent: \(\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y)\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Worked Example: Variance of Sample Mean
text:
Worked Example: Variance of Sample Mean
Problem: If \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) are independent observations with variance \(\sigma^2\), what is \(\text{Var}(\bar{X})\)?

\[\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \text{Var}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right)\]


\[= \frac{1}{n^2} \text{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\right) \quad \text{(Property 2)}\]


\[= \frac{1}{n^2} \sum_{i=1}^n \text{Var}(X_i) \quad \text{(Property 3: independence)}\]


\[= \frac{1}{n^2} \cdot n\sigma^2 = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]






Key Result


The variance of \(\bar{X}\) decreases as sample size \(n\) increases!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
What is a Sampling Distribution?
Different samples give different values of a statistic. The sampling distribution describes this variability.





Sample
Sample Mean (x̄)

10.03

10.85

9.31






Each sample gives a different estimate, but they cluster around the true value \(\mu = 10\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Simulation: Building a Sampling Distribution

# Parameters
true_effect <- 10  # True mean BP reduction (mmHg)
true_sd <- 4       # Standard deviation
n_patients <- 25   # Patients per trial
n_trials <- 5000   # Number of simulated trials

# Simulate many clinical trials
sampling_distribution <- tibble(trial = 1:n_trials) |> 
  mutate(
    sample_mean = map_dbl(trial, \(t) {
      patients <- rnorm(n_patients, true_effect, true_sd)
      mean(patients)
    })
  )

# Visualize
sampling_distribution |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = sample_mean)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7, color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_effect, color = "red", linewidth = 1.5) +
  labs(title = "Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean",
       subtitle = str_glue("True μ = {true_effect}, n = {n_patients}, {n_trials} simulated trials"),
       x = "Sample Mean (estimated BP reduction)", y = "Frequency")

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Why Optimization Matters in Statistics
Many statistical methods require finding the “best” value of a parameter.
Examples:

Maximum Likelihood: Find the parameter value that makes the observed data most probable
Least Squares: Find the parameter value that minimizes prediction errors
Minimum Variance: Find the estimator with the smallest spread


The Problem: How do we find maximums and minimums numerically?

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Optimization: The Graphical Intuition

The maximum occurs where the function reaches its peak.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Concrete Example: Finding the Best Estimate
text:
Concrete Example: Finding the Best Estimate
Scenario: In a clinical trial, 7 out of 10 patients respond to treatment. What’s the best estimate of the true response rate \(p\)?

Approach: Find the value of \(p\) that makes observing “7 out of 10” most likely.
The probability of observing exactly 7 successes in 10 trials is: \[P(X = 7) = \binom{10}{7} p^7 (1-p)^3\]


Question: For what value of \(p\) is this probability largest?

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Grid Search: A Simple Numerical Approach
text:
Grid Search: A Simple Numerical Approach
Idea: Try many values and see which gives the largest result.

# Try different values of p
grid_search <- tibble(p = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |> 
  mutate(
    likelihood = dbinom(7, size = 10, prob = p)
  )

# Find the maximum
grid_search |> 
  slice_max(likelihood, n = 1)

# A tibble: 1 × 2
      p likelihood
  <dbl>      <dbl>
1   0.7      0.267



The maximum likelihood estimate is \(\hat{p} = 0.70 = \frac{7}{10}\). This makes intuitive sense!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Using R’s Optimizer
R has built-in functions to find maximums and minimums more precisely:

# Define the likelihood function
likelihood_function <- function(p) {
  dbinom(7, size = 10, prob = p)
}

# Use optimize() to find the maximum
# Note: optimize finds MINIMUM by default, so we negate for maximum
result <- optimize(
  f = function(p) -likelihood_function(p),  # Negative to find max
  interval = c(0, 1)                         # Search between 0 and 1
)

# The maximum occurs at:
cat("Maximum likelihood estimate: p =", result$minimum)

Maximum likelihood estimate: p = 0.6999843

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
How Numerical Optimization Works

Key idea: The algorithm evaluates the function at different points and iteratively narrows in on the maximum.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Your Turn: Numerical Optimization
Exercise: A diagnostic test correctly identifies a disease in 18 out of 25 patients who have it. Find the maximum likelihood estimate for the test’s sensitivity \(p\).

# Fill in the blanks:
likelihood_fn <- function(p) {
  dbinom(___, size = ___, prob = p)  # What goes here?
}

result <- optimize(
  f = function(p) -likelihood_fn(p),
  interval = c(0, 1)
)

result$minimum  # This is the MLE



# Solution:
likelihood_fn <- function(p) {
  dbinom(18, size = 25, prob = p)
}

result <- optimize(f = function(p) -likelihood_fn(p), interval = c(0, 1))
cat("MLE of sensitivity:", result$minimum)  # Should be 18/25 = 0.72

MLE of sensitivity: 0.7200103

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
When Optimization Gets Harder
Sometimes we need to optimize over multiple parameters or complex functions:

# Example: Finding mean and SD that best fit data
patient_data <- c(120, 135, 128, 142, 131, 125, 138, 129, 133, 127)

# Negative log-likelihood for normal distribution
neg_log_lik <- function(params) {
  mu <- params[1]
  sigma <- params[2]
  if (sigma <= 0) return(Inf)  # sigma must be positive
  -sum(dnorm(patient_data, mean = mu, sd = sigma, log = TRUE))
}

# Use optim() for multiple parameters
result <- optim(par = c(130, 10), fn = neg_log_lik)
cat("MLE for mean:", round(result$par[1], 2), "\n")

MLE for mean: 130.8 

cat("MLE for SD:", round(result$par[2], 2), "\n")

MLE for SD: 6.13 

cat("Compare to sample mean:", round(mean(patient_data), 2))

Compare to sample mean: 130.8

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Lesson 1 Summary
Key Concepts:

Statistical Inference: Using sample data to learn about population parameters
Parameters vs. Statistics:

Parameters (\(\mu\), \(\sigma\), \(p\)): Fixed but unknown population values
Statistics (\(\bar{X}\), \(S\), \(\hat{p}\)): Calculated from sample data

Sampling Distribution: The distribution of a statistic across many samples

\(E(\bar{X}) = \mu\) (centered at population mean)
\(\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \sigma^2/n\) (precision improves with larger \(n\))

Numerical Optimization: Finding maximum/minimum values

Grid search: try many values
optimize(): efficient numerical search

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lesson 3:

MVUE: Best unbiased estimator (smallest variance)
Likelihood function and log-likelihood
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
Efficient estimators achieve the CRLB


Today’s Goals:

Learn to construct estimators systematically
Method of Moments: Simple, intuitive approach
Maximum Likelihood: Powerful, principled approach
Compare the two methods

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Motivating Question
We’ve learned how to evaluate estimators (bias, variance, efficiency).
But how do we construct them in the first place?

Two major methods:

Method of Moments (MME): Match population and sample moments
Maximum Likelihood (MLE): Find parameter that makes data most “likely”









Key Insight


Both methods give us systematic recipes for deriving estimators from any specified distribution.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Population vs. Sample Moments






Definitions (Devore 7.2)


Population Moments:

1st moment: \(E(X) = \mu_1'\)
2nd moment: \(E(X^2) = \mu_2'\)
kth moment: \(E(X^k) = \mu_k'\)

Sample Moments:

1st sample moment: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = \bar{X}\)
2nd sample moment: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2\)
kth sample moment: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Method of Moments Principle






Method of Moments Estimators (MMEs)


To estimate \(m\) unknown parameters \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\):

Express the first \(m\) population moments as functions of the parameters
Set each population moment equal to its sample counterpart
Solve the resulting system of equations for \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\)





The idea: If the population and sample moments should be “close,” we can estimate parameters by equating them.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 1: Exponential Distribution (One Parameter)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\) where \(\lambda\) is the rate parameter.
Goal: Find the MME for \(\lambda\).

Step 1: Population moment: \(E(X) = 1/\lambda\)
Step 2: Set equal to sample moment: \(\frac{1}{\lambda} = \bar{X}\)
Step 3: Solve: \(\hat{\lambda}_{MME} = \frac{1}{\bar{X}}\)








Intuition


If the population mean is \(1/\lambda\), and we estimate the population mean with \(\bar{X}\), then we estimate \(\lambda\) with \(1/\bar{X}\).

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Medical Application: Hospital Wait Times
Emergency room wait times are often modeled with an exponential distribution.

# Wait times (minutes) for 40 patients
wait_times <- c(12, 45, 8, 23, 67, 15, 31, 42, 19, 56,
                28, 11, 38, 22, 49, 17, 33, 25, 41, 14,
                52, 9, 36, 27, 44, 18, 29, 47, 21, 35,
                13, 39, 24, 51, 16, 32, 46, 20, 37, 26)

# Method of moments estimate for λ (per minute)
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(wait_times)

cat("Sample mean wait time:", round(mean(wait_times), 2), "minutes\n")

Sample mean wait time: 30.45 minutes

cat("MME of λ:", round(lambda_hat, 4), "per minute\n")

MME of λ: 0.0328 per minute

cat("MME of λ:", round(lambda_hat * 60, 2), "per hour")

MME of λ: 1.97 per hour

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Verifying with Visualization

# Compare empirical distribution to fitted exponential
tibble(wait_time = wait_times) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = wait_time)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 15, 
                 fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_function(fun = dexp, args = list(rate = lambda_hat),
                color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(title = "ER Wait Times with Fitted Exponential Distribution",
       subtitle = str_glue("MME: λ̂ = {round(lambda_hat, 4)}"),
       x = "Wait Time (minutes)", y = "Density") +
  annotate("text", x = 50, y = 0.025, 
           label = str_glue("Mean = {round(mean(wait_times), 1)} min"),
           color = "red", size = 5)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 2: Normal Distribution (Two Parameters)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
Goal: Find MMEs for \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

Population moments:

\(E(X) = \mu\)
\(E(X^2) = \mu^2 + \sigma^2\) (variance shortcut formula!)



Set equal to sample moments:

\(\mu = \bar{X}\)
\(\mu^2 + \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Solving for the Normal MMEs
From the two equations:
\[\hat{\mu}_{MME} = \bar{X}\]

\[\hat{\sigma}^2_{MME} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\]








Note on Bias


The MME for \(\sigma^2\) divides by \(n\), not \(n-1\). This means the MME is biased!
\[E(\hat{\sigma}^2_{MME}) = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2\]
The usual sample variance \(S^2\) with \(n-1\) in the denominator is unbiased.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 3: Gamma Distribution (Two Parameters)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)\)
Moments:

\(E(X) = \alpha\beta\)
\(E(X^2) = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2\)


MME equations: \[\bar{X} = \alpha\beta\] \[\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2\]


Solutions (after algebra): \[\hat{\alpha} = \frac{\bar{X}^2}{\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2} = \frac{\bar{X}^2}{\hat{\sigma}^2} \quad \quad \hat{\beta} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2}{\bar{X}} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\bar{X}}\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Medical Application: Surgery Recovery Times
Recovery times after surgery often follow a gamma distribution.

# Recovery times (days) for 25 patients
recovery_times <- c(4.2, 6.8, 5.1, 8.3, 7.2, 4.9, 6.1, 9.5, 5.7, 7.8,
                    6.4, 8.1, 5.3, 7.5, 6.9, 4.5, 8.7, 5.9, 7.1, 6.2,
                    9.2, 5.5, 7.4, 6.6, 8.4)

# Calculate sample moments
x_bar <- mean(recovery_times)
second_moment <- mean(recovery_times^2)

# MME for gamma parameters
alpha_hat <- x_bar^2 / (second_moment - x_bar^2)
beta_hat <- (second_moment - x_bar^2) / x_bar

cat("Sample mean:", round(x_bar, 2), "days\n")

Sample mean: 6.77 days

cat("MME of α:", round(alpha_hat, 2), "\n")

MME of α: 22.56 

cat("MME of β:", round(beta_hat, 2), "days")

MME of β: 0.3 days

tibble(recovery_time = recovery_times) |>

  stat_function(fun = dgamma, 
                args = list(shape = alpha_hat, scale = beta_hat),

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Your Turn: Method of Moments
Exercise: Drug concentrations in blood plasma follow a Uniform[0, \(\theta\)] distribution. From \(n = 15\) measurements, you observe \(\bar{x} = 4.2\) mg/L.
Find the MME of \(\theta\).

Solution:
For Uniform[0, \(\theta\)]: \(E(X) = \theta/2\)
Setting equal to sample mean: \(\bar{x} = \theta/2\)
Therefore: \(\hat{\theta}_{MME} = 2\bar{x} = 2(4.2) = 8.4\) mg/L

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: Properties of Method of Moments Estimators
text:
Properties of Method of Moments Estimators
Advantages:

Simple to compute (usually just algebra)
Often has closed-form solutions
Usually consistent (converges to true value as \(n \to \infty\))


Disadvantages:

May not be efficient (doesn’t achieve CRLB)
Can sometimes give impossible values
May be biased









Coming Up Next


Maximum likelihood estimators are often more efficient than MMEs.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Motivating Example: Vaccine Efficacy
A clinical trial for a new vaccine enrolls 200 participants. After exposure to the pathogen, 156 remain disease-free.

Question: What is the true efficacy rate \(p\) of this vaccine?



n <- 200
successes <- 156
# What value of p makes this outcome most "likely"?

Intuition: We should choose the value of \(p\) that makes our observed data “most likely” to have occurred.


This is the essence of Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
From Probability to Likelihood
Probability vs. Likelihood: A Key Distinction

Probability (parameters fixed, data varies):

Given a known parameter value \(\theta\), how likely are different data outcomes?
Example: If \(p = 0.8\), what’s \(P(X = 156)\) out of 200?



Likelihood (data fixed, parameters vary):

Given our observed data, how “likely” are different parameter values?
Example: We observed 156 successes. Which value of \(p\) best explains this?

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Likelihood Function: Definition






Definition (Devore 7.2)


Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) have a joint distribution that depends on parameter \(\theta\). The likelihood function \(L(\theta)\) is this joint distribution, regarded as a function of \(\theta\) (with observed data held fixed).
For a random sample: \[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)\]
where \(f\) is the pmf (discrete) or pdf (continuous).

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Visualizing Likelihood: Binomial Example

The MLE is the value of \(p\) at the peak of the likelihood function.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimate: Definition






Definition


The Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) \(\hat{\theta}\) is the value of \(\theta\) that maximizes the likelihood function:
\[\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_\theta L(\theta)\]
The MLE is the parameter value that makes the observed data “most likely.”




Notation:

\(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE (estimator, a random variable)
\(\hat{\theta}\) is also the observed mle (estimate, a specific number from data)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Why Maximum Likelihood?
Intuitive Appeal:

Choose the parameter that “best explains” our data
The data we observed should be highly probable under the true parameter


Theoretical Properties (more details later):

Consistent: \(\hat{\theta} \to \theta\) as \(n \to \infty\)
Asymptotically unbiased: \(E(\hat{\theta}) \approx \theta\) for large \(n\)
Asymptotically efficient: Achieves smallest possible variance for large \(n\)
Invariance: If \(\hat{\theta}\) is MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat{\theta})\) is MLE of \(g(\theta)\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Why Use Log-Likelihood?
The likelihood function is often a product of many terms: \[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)\]

Taking the logarithm converts products to sums: \[\ell(\theta) = \ln L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln f(x_i; \theta)\]


Key property: Since \(\ln\) is monotonically increasing: \[\arg\max_\theta L(\theta) = \arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta)\]
Maximizing the log-likelihood gives the same answer!

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Advantages of Log-Likelihood
Computational:

Sums are easier to differentiate than products
Avoids numerical underflow (very small products)


Mathematical:

\(\ell'(\theta) = 0\) is often easier to solve
Second derivative test is more tractable

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The General MLE Recipe






Finding the MLE



Write down the likelihood: \(L(\theta) = \prod f(x_i; \theta)\)
Take the logarithm: \(\ell(\theta) = \sum \ln f(x_i; \theta)\)
Differentiate: Find \(\ell'(\theta) = \frac{d\ell}{d\theta}\)
Solve: Set \(\ell'(\theta) = 0\) and solve for \(\hat{\theta}\)
Verify: Check that \(\ell''(\hat{\theta}) < 0\) (maximum, not minimum)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) (iid)
Let \(x = \sum x_i\) be the number of successes.

Step 1 - Likelihood: \[L(p) = \prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i} = p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\]


Step 2 - Log-likelihood: \[\ell(p) = x\ln(p) + (n-x)\ln(1-p)\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli (continued)
Step 3 - Differentiate: \[\ell'(p) = \frac{x}{p} - \frac{n-x}{1-p}\]

Step 4 - Solve: \[\frac{x}{p} = \frac{n-x}{1-p}\] \[x(1-p) = p(n-x)\] \[x - xp = np - xp\] \[x = np\] \[\hat{p} = \frac{x}{n}\]


The MLE is the sample proportion! This matches our intuition.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Simulation: Verifying the Bernoulli MLE

true_p <- 0.65
n <- 50
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulate MLE for many samples
bernoulli_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rbinom(n, 1, true_p)),
    mle = map_dbl(data, mean)
  )

# Check properties
bernoulli_sim |> 
  summarize(
    mean_mle = mean(mle),
    var_mle = var(mle),
    theoretical_var = true_p * (1 - true_p) / n
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_mle var_mle theoretical_var
     <dbl>   <dbl>           <dbl>
1    0.650 0.00450         0.00455

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 2: Exponential Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\)

Likelihood: \[L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i} = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}\]


Log-likelihood: \[\ell(\lambda) = n\ln(\lambda) - \lambda \sum x_i\]


Solve: \[\ell'(\lambda) = \frac{n}{\lambda} - \sum x_i = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\lambda} = \frac{n}{\sum x_i} = \frac{1}{\bar{X}}\]


Same as MME! This is common for exponential family distributions.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 3: Normal Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), both unknown

Log-likelihood: \[\ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\ln(\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i - \mu)^2\]


Partial derivatives: \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mu} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum(x_i - \mu) = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\mu} = \bar{X}\]
\[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \sigma^2} = -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum(x_i - \mu)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{X})^2\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Important Note on Normal MLE
\[\hat{\sigma}^2_{MLE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{X})^2\]







Bias Alert!


The MLE divides by \(n\), not \(n-1\):
\[E(\hat{\sigma}^2_{MLE}) = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2 \neq \sigma^2\]
The MLE is biased for \(\sigma^2\)!





However, for large \(n\), this bias becomes negligible: \[\frac{n-1}{n} \to 1 \text{ as } n \to \infty\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 4: Uniform Distribution (Boundary Solution)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Likelihood: \[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta} \cdot I(0 \le x_i \le \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \le \theta)\]

Key insight: \(L(\theta) = 0\) if \(\theta < \max(x_i)\)


For \(\theta \ge \max(x_i)\): \(L(\theta) = 1/\theta^n\) is decreasing in \(\theta\)


MLE: \(\hat{\theta} = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\)
Derivative method fails! This is a boundary maximum.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
MLE vs MME for Uniform

theta <- 10
n <- 20
n_sims <- 5000

uniform_comparison <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) runif(n, 0, theta)),
    mle = map_dbl(data, max),
    mme = map_dbl(data, \(d) 2 * mean(d))
  )

uniform_comparison |> 
  summarize(
    `MLE Bias` = mean(mle) - theta,
    `MME Bias` = mean(mme) - theta,
    `MLE Variance` = var(mle),
    `MME Variance` = var(mme),
    `MLE MSE` = mean((mle - theta)^2),
    `MME MSE` = mean((mme - theta)^2)
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> 
  mutate(value = round(value, 4))

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  name           value
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 MLE Bias     -0.479 
2 MME Bias      0.0022
3 MLE Variance  0.201 
4 MME Variance  1.61  
5 MLE MSE       0.430 
6 MME MSE       1.61  


The MLE has smaller MSE despite being biased!

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: Visualizing MLE vs MME

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Property 1: Invariance






Invariance Property


If \(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE of \(\theta\), then for any function \(g\):
\[\widehat{g(\theta)} = g(\hat{\theta})\]
The MLE of \(g(\theta)\) is simply \(g\) applied to the MLE of \(\theta\).




Example: If \(\hat{p} = 0.78\) is the MLE for a proportion, then:

MLE of odds \(= p/(1-p)\): \(\hat{\text{odds}} = 0.78/0.22 = 3.55\)
MLE of \(\log(p)\): \(\widehat{\log p} = \log(0.78) = -0.248\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Property 2: Consistency






Theorem


Under general regularity conditions, MLEs are consistent:
\[\hat{\theta} \xrightarrow{P} \theta \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
The MLE converges in probability to the true parameter value.




Intuition: With more data, our estimate gets closer to the truth.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Demonstrating Consistency

true_lambda <- 0.5
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)

consistency_sim <- map_dfr(sample_sizes, function(n) {
  tibble(
    n = n,
    sim = 1:1000,
    mle = map_dbl(sim, \(s) 1 / mean(rexp(n, rate = true_lambda)))
  )
})

consistency_sim |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mle, fill = factor(n))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_lambda, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~n, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_both) +
  labs(title = "Consistency of Exponential MLE",
       subtitle = "Distribution concentrates around true λ = 0.5 as n increases",
       x = "MLE of λ", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Property 3: Asymptotic Normality & Efficiency






Theorem (Devore 7.4)


Under regularity conditions, for large \(n\):

\(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately unbiased: \(E(\hat{\theta}) \approx \theta\)
\(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately normal: \(\hat{\theta} \dot{\sim} N\left(\theta, \frac{1}{nI(\theta)}\right)\)
\(\hat{\theta}\) is asymptotically efficient: Achieves the Cramér-Rao lower bound





In practice: For large samples, the MLE is approximately the MVUE!

text:
Comparing Estimator Properties



Property
MME
MLE




Computation
Usually simple algebra
May require optimization


Bias
Sometimes unbiased
Often biased for small \(n\)


Efficiency

General Guidance



Use MME for quick, rough estimates or simple distributions
Use MLE for final analysis and complex distributions
MLE is generally preferred when computationally feasible

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Computing MLEs in R
Using built-in functions:

# For distributions with known MLEs
normal_data <- rnorm(100, mean = 50, sd = 10)
cat("Normal MLE for μ:", mean(normal_data), "\n")

Normal MLE for μ: 48.41066 

cat("Normal MLE for σ:", sd(normal_data) * sqrt((100-1)/100))

Normal MLE for σ: 10.03329



Using optimization for complex cases:

# General approach: maximize log-likelihood
neg_log_lik <- function(lambda, data) {
  -sum(dexp(data, rate = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

exp_data <- rexp(50, rate = 0.5)
result <- optimize(neg_log_lik, interval = c(0.01, 5), data = exp_data)
cat("\nExponential MLE for λ:", round(result$minimum, 4))


Exponential MLE for λ: 0.5746

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Using fitdistr for Common Distributions

library(MASS)

# Fit various distributions
gamma_data <- rgamma(100, shape = 2, scale = 3)

# Method of moments (manual)
xbar <- mean(gamma_data)
s2 <- var(gamma_data) * (99/100)

beta_mme <- s2 / xbar

# MLE using fitdistr

cat("MME: α =", round(alpha_mme, 3), ", β =", round(beta_mme, 3), "\n")

MME: α = 2.056 , β = 2.871

text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lesson 3:

MVUE: Best unbiased estimator (smallest variance)
Likelihood function and log-likelihood
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
Efficient estimators achieve the CRLB

Learn to construct estimators systematically
Method of Moments: Simple, intuitive approach
Maximum Likelihood: Powerful, principled approach
Compare the two methods

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Motivating Question
We’ve learned how to evaluate estimators (bias, variance, efficiency).
But how do we construct them in the first place?

Two major methods:

Method of Moments (MME): Match population and sample moments
Maximum Likelihood (MLE): Find parameter that makes data most “likely”









Key Insight


Both methods give us systematic recipes for deriving estimators from any specified distribution.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Population vs. Sample Moments






Definitions (Devore 7.2)


Population Moments:

1st moment: \(E(X) = \mu_1'\)
2nd moment: \(E(X^2) = \mu_2'\)
kth moment: \(E(X^k) = \mu_k'\)

Sample Moments:

1st sample moment: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i = \bar{X}\)
2nd sample moment: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^2\)
kth sample moment: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Method of Moments Principle






Method of Moments Estimators (MMEs)


To estimate \(m\) unknown parameters \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\):

Express the first \(m\) population moments as functions of the parameters
Set each population moment equal to its sample counterpart
Solve the resulting system of equations for \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\)





The idea: If the population and sample moments should be “close,” we can estimate parameters by equating them.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 1: Exponential Distribution (One Parameter)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\) where \(\lambda\) is the rate parameter.
Goal: Find the MME for \(\lambda\).

Step 1: Population moment: \(E(X) = 1/\lambda\)
Step 2: Set equal to sample moment: \(\frac{1}{\lambda} = \bar{X}\)
Step 3: Solve: \(\hat{\lambda}_{MME} = \frac{1}{\bar{X}}\)








Intuition


If the population mean is \(1/\lambda\), and we estimate the population mean with \(\bar{X}\), then we estimate \(\lambda\) with \(1/\bar{X}\).

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Medical Application: Hospital Wait Times
Emergency room wait times are often modeled with an exponential distribution.

# Wait times (minutes) for 40 patients
wait_times <- c(12, 45, 8, 23, 67, 15, 31, 42, 19, 56,
                28, 11, 38, 22, 49, 17, 33, 25, 41, 14,
                52, 9, 36, 27, 44, 18, 29, 47, 21, 35,
                13, 39, 24, 51, 16, 32, 46, 20, 37, 26)

# Method of moments estimate for λ (per minute)
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(wait_times)

cat("Sample mean wait time:", round(mean(wait_times), 2), "minutes\n")

Sample mean wait time: 30.45 minutes

cat("MME of λ:", round(lambda_hat, 4), "per minute\n")

MME of λ: 0.0328 per minute

cat("MME of λ:", round(lambda_hat * 60, 2), "per hour")

MME of λ: 1.97 per hour

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 2: Normal Distribution (Two Parameters)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\)
Goal: Find MMEs for \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

Population moments:

\(E(X) = \mu\)
\(E(X^2) = \mu^2 + \sigma^2\) (variance shortcut formula!)



Set equal to sample moments:

\(\mu = \bar{X}\)
\(\mu^2 + \sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Solving for the Normal MMEs
From the two equations:
\[\hat{\mu}_{MME} = \bar{X}\]

\[\hat{\sigma}^2_{MME} = \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(X_i - \bar{X})^2\]








Note on Bias


The MME for \(\sigma^2\) divides by \(n\), not \(n-1\). This means the MME is biased!
\[E(\hat{\sigma}^2_{MME}) = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2\]
The usual sample variance \(S^2\) with \(n-1\) in the denominator is unbiased.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 3: Gamma Distribution (Two Parameters)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Gamma}(\alpha, \beta)\)
Moments:

\(E(X) = \alpha\beta\)
\(E(X^2) = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2\)


MME equations: \[\bar{X} = \alpha\beta\] \[\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 = \alpha(\alpha+1)\beta^2\]


Solutions (after algebra): \[\hat{\alpha} = \frac{\bar{X}^2}{\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2} = \frac{\bar{X}^2}{\hat{\sigma}^2} \quad \quad \hat{\beta} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2 - \bar{X}^2}{\bar{X}} = \frac{\hat{\sigma}^2}{\bar{X}}\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Medical Application: Surgery Recovery Times
Recovery times after surgery often follow a gamma distribution.

# Recovery times (days) for 25 patients
recovery_times <- c(4.2, 6.8, 5.1, 8.3, 7.2, 4.9, 6.1, 9.5, 5.7, 7.8,
                    6.4, 8.1, 5.3, 7.5, 6.9, 4.5, 8.7, 5.9, 7.1, 6.2,
                    9.2, 5.5, 7.4, 6.6, 8.4)

# Calculate sample moments
x_bar <- mean(recovery_times)
second_moment <- mean(recovery_times^2)

# MME for gamma parameters
alpha_hat <- x_bar^2 / (second_moment - x_bar^2)
beta_hat <- (second_moment - x_bar^2) / x_bar

cat("Sample mean:", round(x_bar, 2), "days\n")

Sample mean: 6.77 days

cat("MME of α:", round(alpha_hat, 2), "\n")

MME of α: 22.56 

cat("MME of β:", round(beta_hat, 2), "days")

MME of β: 0.3 days

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Your Turn: Method of Moments
Exercise: Drug concentrations in blood plasma follow a Uniform[0, \(\theta\)] distribution. From \(n = 15\) measurements, you observe \(\bar{x} = 4.2\) mg/L.
Find the MME of \(\theta\).

Solution:
For Uniform[0, \(\theta\)]: \(E(X) = \theta/2\)
Setting equal to sample mean: \(\bar{x} = \theta/2\)
Therefore: \(\hat{\theta}_{MME} = 2\bar{x} = 2(4.2) = 8.4\) mg/L

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
section: Properties of Method of Moments Estimators
text:
Properties of Method of Moments Estimators
Advantages:

Simple to compute (usually just algebra)
Often has closed-form solutions
Usually consistent (converges to true value as \(n \to \infty\))


Disadvantages:

May not be efficient (doesn’t achieve CRLB)
Can sometimes give impossible values
May be biased









Coming Up Next


Maximum likelihood estimators are often more efficient than MMEs.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Motivating Example: Vaccine Efficacy
A clinical trial for a new vaccine enrolls 200 participants. After exposure to the pathogen, 156 remain disease-free.

Question: What is the true efficacy rate \(p\) of this vaccine?



n <- 200
successes <- 156
# What value of p makes this outcome most "likely"?

Intuition: We should choose the value of \(p\) that makes our observed data “most likely” to have occurred.


This is the essence of Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
From Probability to Likelihood
Probability vs. Likelihood: A Key Distinction

Probability (parameters fixed, data varies):

Given a known parameter value \(\theta\), how likely are different data outcomes?
Example: If \(p = 0.8\), what’s \(P(X = 156)\) out of 200?



Likelihood (data fixed, parameters vary):

Given our observed data, how “likely” are different parameter values?
Example: We observed 156 successes. Which value of \(p\) best explains this?

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The Likelihood Function: Definition






Definition (Devore 7.2)


Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) have a joint distribution that depends on parameter \(\theta\). The likelihood function \(L(\theta)\) is this joint distribution, regarded as a function of \(\theta\) (with observed data held fixed).
For a random sample: \[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)\]
where \(f\) is the pmf (discrete) or pdf (continuous).

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Visualizing Likelihood: Code

# Likelihood function for vaccine trial
n <- 200
x <- 156

likelihood_data <- tibble(
  p = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.001),
  likelihood = dbinom(x, n, p)
)

mle_p <- x / n

likelihood_data |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = likelihood)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mle_p, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(x = mle_p, y = dbinom(x, n, mle_p)), color = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(title = "Likelihood Function for Vaccine Efficacy",
       subtitle = str_glue("Observed: {x} successes out of {n} participants"),
       x = "Efficacy Parameter (p)", y = "Likelihood L(p)") +
  annotate("text", x = mle_p + 0.08, y = dbinom(x, n, mle_p) * 0.9,
           label = str_glue("MLE: p̂ = {mle_p}"), color = "red", size = 5)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Visualizing Likelihood: Result

The MLE is the value of \(p\) at the peak of the likelihood function.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Maximum Likelihood Estimate: Definition






Definition


The Maximum Likelihood Estimate (MLE) \(\hat{\theta}\) is the value of \(\theta\) that maximizes the likelihood function:
\[\hat{\theta} = \arg\max_\theta L(\theta)\]
The MLE is the parameter value that makes the observed data “most likely.”




Notation:

\(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE (estimator, a random variable)
\(\hat{\theta}\) is also the observed mle (estimate, a specific number from data)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Why Maximum Likelihood?
Intuitive Appeal:

Choose the parameter that “best explains” our data
The data we observed should be highly probable under the true parameter


Theoretical Properties (more details later):

Consistent: \(\hat{\theta} \to \theta\) as \(n \to \infty\)
Asymptotically unbiased: \(E(\hat{\theta}) \approx \theta\) for large \(n\)
Asymptotically efficient: Achieves smallest possible variance for large \(n\)
Invariance: If \(\hat{\theta}\) is MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat{\theta})\) is MLE of \(g(\theta)\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Why Use Log-Likelihood?
The likelihood function is often a product of many terms: \[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)\]

Taking the logarithm converts products to sums: \[\ell(\theta) = \ln L(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln f(x_i; \theta)\]


Key property: Since \(\ln\) is monotonically increasing: \[\arg\max_\theta L(\theta) = \arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta)\]
Maximizing the log-likelihood gives the same answer!

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Advantages of Log-Likelihood
Computational:

Sums are easier to differentiate than products
Avoids numerical underflow (very small products)


Mathematical:

\(\ell'(\theta) = 0\) is often easier to solve
Second derivative test is more tractable

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text: Likelihood vs. Log-Likelihood: Result

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
The General MLE Recipe






Finding the MLE



Write down the likelihood: \(L(\theta) = \prod f(x_i; \theta)\)
Take the logarithm: \(\ell(\theta) = \sum \ln f(x_i; \theta)\)
Differentiate: Find \(\ell'(\theta) = \frac{d\ell}{d\theta}\)
Solve: Set \(\ell'(\theta) = 0\) and solve for \(\hat{\theta}\)
Verify: Check that \(\ell''(\hat{\theta}) < 0\) (maximum, not minimum)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) (iid)
Let \(x = \sum x_i\) be the number of successes.

Step 1 - Likelihood: \[L(p) = \prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i} = p^x(1-p)^{n-x}\]


Step 2 - Log-likelihood: \[\ell(p) = x\ln(p) + (n-x)\ln(1-p)\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli (continued)
Step 3 - Differentiate: \[\ell'(p) = \frac{x}{p} - \frac{n-x}{1-p}\]

Step 4 - Solve: \[\frac{x}{p} = \frac{n-x}{1-p}\] \[x(1-p) = p(n-x)\] \[x - xp = np - xp\] \[x = np\] \[\hat{p} = \frac{x}{n}\]


The MLE is the sample proportion! This matches our intuition.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Simulation: Verifying the Bernoulli MLE

true_p <- 0.65
n <- 50
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulate MLE for many samples
bernoulli_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rbinom(n, 1, true_p)),
    mle = map_dbl(data, mean)
  )

# Check properties
bernoulli_sim |> 
  summarize(
    mean_mle = mean(mle),
    var_mle = var(mle),
    theoretical_var = true_p * (1 - true_p) / n
  )

# A tibble: 1 × 3
  mean_mle var_mle theoretical_var
     <dbl>   <dbl>           <dbl>
1    0.650 0.00450         0.00455

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 2: Exponential Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\)

Likelihood: \[L(\lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i} = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}\]


Log-likelihood: \[\ell(\lambda) = n\ln(\lambda) - \lambda \sum x_i\]


Solve: \[\ell'(\lambda) = \frac{n}{\lambda} - \sum x_i = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\lambda} = \frac{n}{\sum x_i} = \frac{1}{\bar{X}}\]


Same as MME! This is common for exponential family distributions.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 3: Normal Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), both unknown

Log-likelihood: \[\ell(\mu, \sigma^2) = -\frac{n}{2}\ln(2\pi) - \frac{n}{2}\ln(\sigma^2) - \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum(x_i - \mu)^2\]


Partial derivatives: \[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \mu} = \frac{1}{\sigma^2}\sum(x_i - \mu) = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\mu} = \bar{X}\]
\[\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial \sigma^2} = -\frac{n}{2\sigma^2} + \frac{1}{2\sigma^4}\sum(x_i - \mu)^2 = 0 \Rightarrow \hat{\sigma}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{X})^2\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Important Note on Normal MLE
\[\hat{\sigma}^2_{MLE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum(x_i - \bar{X})^2\]







Bias Alert!


The MLE divides by \(n\), not \(n-1\):
\[E(\hat{\sigma}^2_{MLE}) = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2 \neq \sigma^2\]
The MLE is biased for \(\sigma^2\)!





However, for large \(n\), this bias becomes negligible: \[\frac{n-1}{n} \to 1 \text{ as } n \to \infty\]

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Example 4: Uniform Distribution (Boundary Solution)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Likelihood: \[L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta} \cdot I(0 \le x_i \le \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \le \theta)\]

Key insight: \(L(\theta) = 0\) if \(\theta < \max(x_i)\)


For \(\theta \ge \max(x_i)\): \(L(\theta) = 1/\theta^n\) is decreasing in \(\theta\)


MLE: \(\hat{\theta} = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\)
Derivative method fails! This is a boundary maximum.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
MLE vs MME for Uniform

theta <- 10
n <- 20
n_sims <- 5000

uniform_comparison <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) runif(n, 0, theta)),
    mle = map_dbl(data, max),
    mme = map_dbl(data, \(d) 2 * mean(d))
  )

uniform_comparison |> 
  summarize(
    `MLE Bias` = mean(mle) - theta,
    `MME Bias` = mean(mme) - theta,
    `MLE Variance` = var(mle),
    `MME Variance` = var(mme),
    `MLE MSE` = mean((mle - theta)^2),
    `MME MSE` = mean((mme - theta)^2)
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> 
  mutate(value = round(value, 4))

# A tibble: 6 × 2
  name           value
  <chr>          <dbl>
1 MLE Bias     -0.479 
2 MME Bias      0.0022
3 MLE Variance  0.201 
4 MME Variance  1.61  
5 MLE MSE       0.430 
6 MME MSE       1.61  


The MLE has smaller MSE despite being biased!

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Property 1: Invariance






Invariance Property


If \(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE of \(\theta\), then for any function \(g\):
\[\widehat{g(\theta)} = g(\hat{\theta})\]
The MLE of \(g(\theta)\) is simply \(g\) applied to the MLE of \(\theta\).




Example: If \(\hat{p} = 0.78\) is the MLE for a proportion, then:

MLE of odds \(= p/(1-p)\): \(\hat{\text{odds}} = 0.78/0.22 = 3.55\)
MLE of \(\log(p)\): \(\widehat{\log p} = \log(0.78) = -0.248\)

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Property 2: Consistency — The Big Picture






What Does Consistency Mean?


An estimator \(\hat{\theta}\) is consistent for \(\theta\) if, as we collect more and more data, our estimate gets closer and closer to the true value.
In plain English: With enough data, we can estimate \(\theta\) as accurately as we want.




Think of it like this:

With \(n = 10\) observations, your estimate might be off by a lot
With \(n = 100\) observations, your estimate is probably closer
With \(n = 1000\) observations, your estimate is very close
As \(n \to \infty\), your estimate essentially equals the truth

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Consistency: A Medical Analogy
Imagine estimating the true cure rate \(p\) of a new drug:



Sample Size
Your Estimate
How Close?




\(n = 10\)
\(\hat{p} = 0.60\)
Could be quite far off


\(n = 100\)
\(\hat{p} = 0.72\)
Getting closer


\(n = 1,000\)
\(\hat{p} = 0.748\)
Very close


\(n = 10,000\)
\(\hat{p} = 0.7502\)
Almost exactly right




If the true cure rate is \(p = 0.75\), a consistent estimator will eventually “find” this value.








Key Insight


Consistency is about what happens as sample size grows—it’s a long-run guarantee about the behavior of an estimator.

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Consistency: Formal Statement






Theorem: MLEs are Consistent


Under general regularity conditions, the MLE \(\hat{\theta}\) satisfies:
\[\hat{\theta} \xrightarrow{P} \theta \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
Translation: For any tolerance \(\epsilon > 0\), no matter how small:
\[P(|\hat{\theta} - \theta| < \epsilon) \to 1 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
The probability that our estimate is within \(\epsilon\) of the truth approaches 100%.




What this does NOT mean:

It does NOT mean \(\hat{\theta}\) is unbiased
It does NOT mean \(\hat{\theta}\) is exactly right for any finite \(n\)
It’s a statement about the limiting behavior as \(n\) grows

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Visualizing Consistency: Setup
Let’s see consistency in action with the Exponential MLE.
True parameter: \(\lambda = 0.5\)
MLE: \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\)
We’ll simulate 1000 MLEs at each sample size and watch the distribution “shrink” around the truth.

true_lambda <- 0.5
sample_sizes <- c(10, 30, 100, 300, 1000)
set.seed(100)

consistency_sim <- map(sample_sizes, function(sample_n) {
  tibble(
    n = sample_n,
    sim = 1:1000,
    mle = map_dbl(sim, \(s) 1 / mean(rexp(sample_n, rate = true_lambda)))
  )
}) %>%
  list_rbind()

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Visualizing Consistency: Code

consistency_sim |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = mle, fill = factor(n))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = true_lambda, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~n, scales = "free_y", labeller = label_both) +
  labs(title = "Consistency of Exponential MLE",
       subtitle = "Distribution concentrates around true λ = 0.5 as n increases",
       x = "MLE of λ", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

text:
Consistency: What the Simulation Shows

# Summarize the spread at each sample size
consistency_sim |> 
  group_by(n) |> 
  summarize(
    mean_estimate = mean(mle),
    sd_estimate = sd(mle),
    pct_within_10pct = mean(abs(mle - true_lambda) < 0.05) * 100
  ) |>

1    10         0.551       0.195             24.7

Observations:

The standard deviation shrinks as \(n\) increases

The mean estimate approaches the true value

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Property 3: Asymptotic Normality & Efficiency






Theorem (Devore 7.4)


Under regularity conditions, for large \(n\):

\(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately unbiased: \(E(\hat{\theta}) \approx \theta\)
\(\hat{\theta}\) is approximately normal: \(\hat{\theta} \dot{\sim} N\left(\theta, \frac{1}{nI(\theta)}\right)\)
\(\hat{\theta}\) is asymptotically efficient: Achieves the Cramér-Rao lower bound





In practice: For large samples, the MLE is approximately the MVUE!

Property
MME

Usually simple algebra

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Computing MLEs in R
Using built-in functions:

# For distributions with known MLEs
normal_data <- rnorm(100, mean = 50, sd = 10)
cat("Normal MLE for μ:", mean(normal_data), "\n")

Normal MLE for μ: 50.91004 

cat("Normal MLE for σ:", sd(normal_data) * sqrt((100-1)/100))

Normal MLE for σ: 9.881601



Using optimization for complex cases:

# General approach: maximize log-likelihood
neg_log_lik <- function(lambda, data) {
  -sum(dexp(data, rate = lambda, log = TRUE))
}

exp_data <- rexp(50, rate = 0.5)
result <- optimize(neg_log_lik, interval = c(0.01, 5), data = exp_data)
cat("\nExponential MLE for λ:", round(result$minimum, 4))


Exponential MLE for λ: 0.4593

title: Lesson 4: Method of Moments and Maximum Likelihood Estimation
text:
Using fitdistr for Common Distributions

library(MASS)

# Fit various distributions
gamma_data <- rgamma(100, shape = 2, scale = 3)

# Method of moments (manual)
xbar <- mean(gamma_data)
s2 <- var(gamma_data) * (99/100)
alpha_mme <- xbar^2 / s2
beta_mme <- s2 / xbar

# MLE using fitdistr
gamma_mle <- fitdistr(gamma_data, "gamma")

cat("MME: α =", round(alpha_mme, 3), ", β =", round(beta_mme, 3), "\n")

MME: α = 1.979 , β = 3.144 

cat("MLE: α =", round(gamma_mle$estimate["shape"], 3), 
    ", β =", round(1/gamma_mle$estimate["rate"], 3))

MLE: α = 2.015 , β = 3.087

Medical Application: Survival Analysis
Cancer survival times are often modeled with exponential or Weibull distributions.

# Survival times (months) for 40 patients
survival_times <- c(8.2, 15.3, 12.1, 6.8, 22.5, 9.4, 18.7, 11.3, 7.5, 25.1,
                    14.2, 10.8, 5.3, 19.6, 13.4, 8.9, 16.2, 11.7, 6.1, 21.3,

Your Turn: MLE Practice
Exercise: A diagnostic test is administered to 80 patients. 64 test positive. Assuming the number positive follows a Binomial distribution, find:

The MLE of the sensitivity \(p\)
The MLE of the odds of a positive result, \(p/(1-p)\)

title: Welcome to BSTA 551!
text:
Structure for this course

Statistics is based on mathematics, which has theoretical underpinnings.
Understanding the “why” behind why we perform certain hypothesis tests and where our estimates come from.
Think of this course as paired with the applied courses. There may be a lot of overlap, but we are going deeper with the “why” and “how”
This used to be two quarters of material, with more proofs and much more calculus. I tried to make this course more digestible in 10 weeks, while also including some simulation/boostrap/permutation methods. Therefore: topics will go by quickly!! We won’t have time to prove most things, you will have to take a lot of this on face value.

 

I agree with Dr. Wakim: “It is going to feel useless at times, but I swear it is not!”
