title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-4:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\), \(\text{MSE} = \text{Var} + \text{Bias}^2\)
MVUE: Unbiased estimator with minimum variance
Fisher Information: \(I(\theta) = E[-\ell''(\theta)]\)
Cramér-Rao Lower Bound: \(\text{Var}(T) \geq 1/I_n(\theta)\)
MLE and MME: Systematic methods for constructing estimators


Today’s Goals:

Understand sufficient statistics: data reduction without information loss
Learn the Neyman Factorization Theorem
Connect sufficiency to finding MVUEs via Rao-Blackwell
Define completeness and its role in optimal estimation

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Motivating Question: Data Reduction
Suppose we observe \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) from a distribution with unknown \(\theta\).
Question: Can we summarize the data with a simpler statistic \(T(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) without losing information about \(\theta\)?







The Key Insight


If a statistic captures all the information about \(\theta\) contained in the data, we call it sufficient for \(\theta\).





Why this matters:

Simplifies analysis and computation
Guides us to optimal estimators
Fundamental for understanding MVUEs

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Mean?
Imagine you’re a consulting statistician. A colleague ran an experiment and wants your help estimating \(\theta\).
Scenario 1: They give you all raw data: \(x_1 = 1, x_2 = 0, x_3 = 3\)
Scenario 2: They only tell you the total: \(T = x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 4\)

Question: Does Scenario 1 give you more information about \(\theta\) than Scenario 2?


If the answer is no—if knowing \(T\) tells you everything about \(\theta\)—then \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Defects (Devore 7.25)
Setup: The number of major defects on new vehicles follows \(\text{Poisson}(\mu)\). We observe \(n = 3\) vehicles with defects \(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0, X_3 = 3\).
Key Question: Would knowing only \(T = \sum X_i = 4\) provide the same information about \(\mu\) as knowing all individual \(X_i\)’s?

Consider: Given that \(T = 4\), what’s the conditional distribution of \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\)?
For the specific triple \((2, 1, 1)\):
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1)}{P(T = 4)}\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson (continued)
\[P(X_1 = 2, X_2 = 1, X_3 = 1 | T = 4) = \frac{\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^2}{2!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!} \cdot \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^1}{1!}}{\frac{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4}{4!}}\]

\[= \frac{e^{-3\mu}\mu^4 / 2}{e^{-3\mu}(3\mu)^4/24} = \frac{24}{2 \cdot 81} = \frac{4}{27}\]








Critical Observation


The \(\mu\) terms cancel out! The conditional probability doesn’t depend on \(\mu\).



This means: once we know \(T = 4\), the specific \((X_1, X_2, X_3)\) values provide no additional information about \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T = t\) does not depend on \(\theta\), for every possible value \(t\).




In other words: Once you know the value of \(T\), the distribution of the data no longer involves \(\theta\)—so no additional information about \(\theta\) can be extracted.








Intuition


\(T\) is sufficient if it “captures” all the information in the data relevant to \(\theta\). It’s sufficient to know \(T\); the raw data adds nothing more.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why is Sufficiency Important?
Practical Implications:

Data Reduction: Sufficient statistics compress data without information loss
Estimator Selection: Any good estimator should depend on the data only through sufficient statistics
Path to MVUE: Combined with other properties, leads to minimum variance estimators


Historical Note: The concept was developed by R.A. Fisher in the 1920s as part of the foundations of modern statistical inference.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Finding Sufficient Statistics: The Challenge
The definition of sufficiency requires computing conditional distributions—which can be quite difficult!

We need a shortcut…


Fortunately, the Neyman Factorization Theorem provides an elegant criterion based on the likelihood function.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Neyman Factorization Theorem






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)


Let \(f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta)\) denote the joint pmf or pdf of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\). Then \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\) if and only if there exist functions \(g\) and \(h\) such that:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) depends on the data only through \(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and involves \(\theta\)
\(h\) depends on the data but not on \(\theta\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Understanding the Factorization
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \underbrace{g(t(x_1, \ldots, x_n); \theta)}_{\text{Involves } \theta \text{ and data through } T} \cdot \underbrace{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}_{\text{Depends on data, not } \theta}\]

Key insight: All information about \(\theta\) is in the \(g\) factor, which depends on \(x_i\)’s only through \(T\).








Strategy for Finding Sufficient Statistics



Write down the joint pmf/pdf
Identify the part that involves \(\theta\)
Factor it so \(\theta\) appears only with a function of the data
That function is your sufficient statistic!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 1: Bernoulli Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Bernoulli}(p)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; p) = \prod_{i=1}^n p^{x_i}(1-p)^{1-x_i} = p^{\sum x_i}(1-p)^{n - \sum x_i}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{p^t(1-p)^{n-t}}_{g(t; p)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) (equivalently, \(\bar{X}\)) is sufficient for \(p\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 2: Poisson Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^t}_{g(t; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod_{i=1}^n x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 3: Exponential Distribution
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\) with pdf \(f(x; \lambda) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \lambda) = \prod_{i=1}^n \lambda e^{-\lambda x_i} = \lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}\]

Factorization: \[= \underbrace{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda t}}_{g(t; \lambda)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \sum_{i=1}^n x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) (equivalently, \(\bar{X}\)) is sufficient for \(\lambda\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Medical Application: Time to Disease Relapse
text:
Medical Application: Time to Disease Relapse
Cancer relapse times are often modeled with exponential distributions.

# Simulated relapse times (months) for 15 patients
set.seed(123)
true_lambda <- 0.1  # Rate parameter (relapses per month)
relapse_times <- rexp(15, rate = true_lambda)

# Sufficient statistic
T_sum <- sum(relapse_times)
T_mean <- mean(relapse_times)

cat("Individual relapse times:\n")

Individual relapse times:

cat(round(relapse_times, 2), "\n\n")

8.43 5.77 13.29 0.32 0.56 3.17 3.14 1.45 27.26 0.29 10.05 4.8 2.81 3.77 1.88 

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σx_i:", round(T_sum, 2), "months\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σx_i: 87 months

cat("Equivalently, x̄ =", round(T_mean, 2), "months\n")

Equivalently, x̄ = 5.8 months

cat("MLE of λ = 1/x̄ =", round(1/T_mean, 4), "per month")

MLE of λ = 1/x̄ = 0.1724 per month

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example 4: Uniform Distribution (Devore 7.27)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{\theta} \cdot I(0 \leq x_i \leq \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta) \cdot I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)\]

Factorization: Using indicator notation: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(t; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(t = \max(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\).








Result


\(T = \max(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\). Note: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient here!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Uniform Example: Visualization

Only the maximum observation matters for estimating \(\theta\)!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?
Consider two datasets with the same mean but different maxima:

# Two samples with same mean but different maxima
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)  # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10) # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 



These have the same \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)



Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses information about \(\theta\)!
The maximum captures information that the mean cannot.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Your Turn: Finding Sufficient Statistics
Exercise: Let \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim \text{Geometric}(p)\) with pmf \(f(x; p) = (1-p)^{x-1}p\) for \(x = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)
Find a sufficient statistic for \(p\).

Solution:
\[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; p) = \prod_{i=1}^n (1-p)^{x_i - 1}p = p^n (1-p)^{\sum x_i - n}\]
\[= \underbrace{p^n (1-p)^{t - n}}_{g(t; p)} \cdot \underbrace{1}_{h}\]
where \(t = \sum x_i\).


Result: \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(p\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
When One Statistic Isn’t Enough
When there are multiple parameters, we typically need multiple sufficient statistics.







Definition: Jointly Sufficient Statistics


Statistics \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) are jointly sufficient for parameters \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\) if the conditional distribution of \(X_1, \ldots, X_n\) given \(T_1 = t_1, \ldots, T_k = t_k\) does not depend on any of the \(\theta_j\)’s.





Factorization Theorem (Extended): \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m) = g(t_1, \ldots, t_k; \theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Normal Distribution (Both Parameters Unknown)
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\) unknown.
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu, \sigma^2) = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\right)^n \exp\left(-\frac{\sum(x_i - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

Expanding \(\sum(x_i - \mu)^2 = \sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2\):
\[= \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)\]

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Normal Distribution (continued)
\[f = \underbrace{\frac{1}{\sigma^n} \exp\left(-\frac{\sum x_i^2 - 2\mu \sum x_i + n\mu^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)}_{g(t_1, t_2; \mu, \sigma^2)} \cdot \underbrace{\left(\frac{1}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}}_{h}\]







Result


\(T_1 = \sum X_i\) (or \(\bar{X}\)) and \(T_2 = \sum X_i^2\) are jointly sufficient for \((\mu, \sigma^2)\).
Equivalently, \((\bar{X}, S^2)\) are jointly sufficient.





Intuition: For normal data, the sample mean and sample variance capture all information about \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Medical Application: Blood Pressure Measurements

# Systolic blood pressure measurements (mmHg) from 30 hypertension patients
set.seed(789)
bp_data <- rnorm(30, mean = 145, sd = 15)

# Jointly sufficient statistics for (μ, σ²)
T1 <- sum(bp_data)
T2 <- sum(bp_data^2)

# Equivalent sufficient statistics
x_bar <- mean(bp_data)
s_squared <- var(bp_data)

cat("Jointly sufficient statistics:\n")

Jointly sufficient statistics:

cat("T₁ = Σxᵢ =", round(T1, 1), "\n")

T₁ = Σxᵢ = 4223.6 

cat("T₂ = Σxᵢ² =", round(T2, 1), "\n\n")

T₂ = Σxᵢ² = 597896 

cat("Equivalent form:\n")

Equivalent form:

cat("x̄ =", round(x_bar, 2), "mmHg\n")

x̄ = 140.79 mmHg

cat("S² =", round(s_squared, 2), "mmHg²")

S² = 113 mmHg²

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: The Problem: Non-Uniqueness of Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Problem: Non-Uniqueness of Sufficient Statistics
Sufficient statistics are not unique!

Trivial example: The entire dataset \((X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is always sufficient.
Less trivial: If \(T\) is sufficient, so is any one-to-one function of \(T\) (e.g., if \(\sum X_i\) is sufficient, so is \(\bar{X}\)).


Question: What is the “best” or “most efficient” sufficient statistic?








Idea


We want the sufficient statistic that achieves the greatest data reduction while still capturing all information about \(\theta\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Definition: Minimal Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A sufficient statistic \(T\) is minimal sufficient if it is a function of every other sufficient statistic.
Equivalently: \(T\) is minimal sufficient if, for any other sufficient statistic \(T'\), we can write \(T = f(T')\) for some function \(f\).




Intuition: A minimal sufficient statistic represents the maximum possible data reduction without losing information about \(\theta\).


Example: For \(N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with both unknown, \((\bar{X}, S^2)\) are jointly minimal sufficient—you cannot reduce the data any further without losing information.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Finding Minimal Sufficient Statistics






Practical Criterion (Devore Exercise 7.74)


\(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is minimal sufficient if for any two sample points \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_n)\) and \(\mathbf{y} = (y_1, \ldots, y_n)\):
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{x}; \theta)}{f(\mathbf{y}; \theta)} \text{ doesn't depend on } \theta \iff t(\mathbf{x}) = t(\mathbf{y})\]




In words: The likelihood ratio is constant in \(\theta\) if and only if the two samples have the same value of \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Minimal Sufficiency for Exponential
For \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Exponential}(\lambda)\):
\[\frac{f(\mathbf{x}; \lambda)}{f(\mathbf{y}; \lambda)} = \frac{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum x_i}}{\lambda^n e^{-\lambda \sum y_i}} = e^{-\lambda(\sum x_i - \sum y_i)}\]

This ratio doesn’t depend on \(\lambda\) \(\iff\) \(\sum x_i = \sum y_i\).


Therefore: \(T = \sum X_i\) is minimal sufficient for \(\lambda\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
A Cautionary Example: Cauchy Distribution
The Cauchy distribution with location parameter \(\theta\) has pdf: \[f(x; \theta) = \frac{1}{\pi[1 + (x - \theta)^2]}\]

For a random sample from Cauchy:

The ordered values \((X_{(1)}, \ldots, X_{(n)})\) are jointly sufficient
Remarkably, the ordered values are also minimal sufficient!









Surprising Result


For Cauchy, there is no reduction from the ordered sample to a simpler statistic. The full ordered data is needed to capture all information about \(\theta\).



This shows that the number of minimal sufficient statistics doesn’t always equal the number of parameters.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters for Estimation
We’ve established that sufficient statistics capture all information about \(\theta\).
Key Question: How do we use this to find better estimators?

The Rao-Blackwell Theorem provides the answer: it shows how to improve any estimator by conditioning on sufficient statistics.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Rao-Blackwell Theorem






Theorem (Rao-Blackwell)


Suppose:

\(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\)
\(U\) is any unbiased estimator for \(h(\theta)\)

Then the estimator \(U^* = E(U | T)\) satisfies:

\(U^*\) is unbiased for \(h(\theta)\)
\(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\)

with strict inequality unless \(U\) is already a function of \(T\).




In words: Conditioning an unbiased estimator on a sufficient statistic never increases variance and often decreases it.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Proof Sketch: Why Rao-Blackwell Works
Step 1: \(U^*\) is an estimator (doesn’t depend on \(\theta\))
Since \(T\) is sufficient, the conditional distribution of \(U | T\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\). Therefore \(E(U | T)\) doesn’t involve \(\theta\). ✓

Step 2: \(U^*\) is unbiased
By the Law of Total Expectation: \[E(U^*) = E[E(U | T)] = E(U) = h(\theta) \checkmark\]


Step 3: \(U^*\) has smaller variance
By the Law of Total Variance: \[\text{Var}(U) = \text{Var}(E[U|T]) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)] = \text{Var}(U^*) + E[\text{Var}(U|T)]\]
Since \(E[\text{Var}(U|T)] \geq 0\), we have \(\text{Var}(U) \geq \text{Var}(U^*)\). ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Poisson Zero-Defect Probability (Devore 7.30)
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\).
Start with a crude unbiased estimator: \[U = I(X_1 = 0) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } X_1 = 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } X_1 > 0 \end{cases}\]

Check: \(E(U) = P(X_1 = 0) = e^{-\mu}\) ✓ (Unbiased!)


Apply Rao-Blackwell: The sufficient statistic is \(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\).
We need: \(U^* = E(U | T) = P(X_1 = 0 | T = t)\)

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Poisson Example (continued)
\[P(X_1 = 0 | T = t) = \frac{P(X_1 = 0 \cap T = t)}{P(T = t)} = \frac{P(X_1 = 0) \cdot P(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i = t)}{P(T = t)}\]

Using the fact that \(\sum_{i=2}^n X_i \sim \text{Poisson}((n-1)\mu)\):
\[= \frac{e^{-\mu} \cdot \frac{e^{-(n-1)\mu}[(n-1)\mu]^t}{t!}}{\frac{e^{-n\mu}(n\mu)^t}{t!}} = \frac{(n-1)^t}{n^t} = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^t\]








Improved Estimator


\[U^* = \left(1 - \frac{1}{n}\right)^T\] is unbiased for \(e^{-\mu}\) with variance \(\leq\) the variance of the crude indicator!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Simulation: Comparing Estimators


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5
n <- 10
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulate Poisson samples and compute estimators
poisson_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),  # I(X_1 = 0)
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum,  # Rao-Blackwell improved
    mle = exp(-T_sum/n)  # MLE of e^(-μ)
  )

# True value
true_prob <- exp(-mu_true)

# Compare estimators
comparison <- poisson_sim |> 
  summarize(
    `E(Crude U)` = mean(crude_U),
    `E(Improved U*)` = mean(improved_U),
    `E(MLE)` = mean(mle),
    `Var(Crude U)` = var(crude_U),
    `Var(Improved U*)` = var(improved_U),
    `Var(MLE)` = var(mle)
  )

cat("True P(X = 0) = e^(-μ) =", round(true_prob, 4), "\n\n")


True P(X = 0) = e^(-μ) = 0.2231

text: Visualization: Rao-Blackwell Improvement

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
section: Key Implication: Best Estimators Use Sufficient Statistics
text:
Key Implication: Best Estimators Use Sufficient Statistics






Corollary of Rao-Blackwell


Any estimator that is not based purely on sufficient statistics is necessarily inferior to some other estimator.




Example: For Uniform\([0, \theta]\), \(\max(X_i)\) is sufficient. Any estimator using \(\bar{X}\) or \(S\) alone is suboptimal:

\(\hat{\theta}_1 = 2\bar{X}\) has variance \(\theta^2/(3n)\)
\(\hat{\theta}_2 = \frac{n+1}{n}\max(X_i)\) has variance \(\theta^2/[n(n+2)]\)

Since \(\bar{X}\) isn’t a function of \(\max(X_i)\), estimator \(\hat{\theta}_1\) loses information!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
MLEs and Sufficient Statistics






Theorem (MLEs Use Sufficient Statistics)


If \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) are jointly sufficient for \(\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_m\), then the MLEs \(\hat{\theta}_1, \ldots, \hat{\theta}_m\) can be expressed as functions of \(T_1, \ldots, T_k\) alone.




Why? The likelihood factors as \(L(\theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\). Maximizing \(L\) is equivalent to maximizing \(g\), which depends on the data only through \(T\).


Practical implication: MLEs automatically “use” sufficient statistics—this is one reason they have such good properties!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Final Piece: Completeness
We’ve seen that:

Sufficient statistics capture all information about \(\theta\)
Rao-Blackwell lets us improve estimators by conditioning on sufficient statistics


Question: Given a sufficient statistic \(T\), is there a unique best unbiased estimator based on \(T\)?


The answer involves completeness—a property that ensures uniqueness.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Definition of Completeness






Definition: Complete Statistic


A statistic \(T\) is complete for \(\theta\) if for any function \(g\):
\[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]
In other words, the only function of \(T\) with expected value 0 for all \(\theta\) is the zero function (almost surely).




Intuition: Completeness means there are “no redundancies” in \(T\)—you can’t construct a non-trivial unbiased estimator of zero using \(T\).

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Why Completeness Matters






Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem


If \(T\) is a complete sufficient statistic and \(U = h(T)\) is an unbiased estimator of \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(U\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).




Proof Sketch:
Suppose \(U_1\) and \(U_2\) are both unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\) and are functions of \(T\).
Then \(E[U_1 - U_2] = 0\) for all \(\theta\).
By completeness, \(U_1 - U_2 = 0\) almost surely.
Therefore \(U_1 = U_2\)—uniqueness! ✓

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Completeness in Exponential Families






Theorem


For distributions in the exponential family (which includes Normal, Poisson, Exponential, Binomial, Gamma), the natural sufficient statistics are typically complete.




Examples of complete sufficient statistics:



Distribution
Complete Sufficient Statistic




Bernoulli\((p)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Poisson\((\mu)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Exponential\((\lambda)\)
\(\sum X_i\)


Normal\((\mu, \sigma^2)\)
\((\bar{X}, S^2)\) jointly

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Example: Normal Mean (Known Variance)
For \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2\) known:

\(\bar{X}\) is sufficient for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{X}\) is complete for \(\mu\)
\(\bar{X}\) is unbiased for \(\mu\)


By Lehmann-Scheffé: \(\bar{X}\) is the unique MVUE of \(\mu\).








The Power of Completeness + Sufficiency


Once we find a complete sufficient statistic, any unbiased function of it is automatically the MVUE!

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
The Road to MVUE: Summary






Alternative path: Use Cramér-Rao bound to verify an estimator achieves minimum variance.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 1: Disease Incidence Rate
Scenario: Epidemiologists count disease cases in \(n\) geographic regions.
Let \(X_i \sim \text{Poisson}(\mu)\) = cases in region \(i\).

# Disease cases in 8 regions
disease_cases <- c(3, 5, 2, 7, 4, 6, 3, 5)
n <- length(disease_cases)

# Sufficient statistic
T_total <- sum(disease_cases)

# MVUE of μ
mu_hat <- mean(disease_cases)

# MVUE of P(no cases) = e^(-μ)
prob_zero_hat <- (1 - 1/n)^T_total

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ =", T_total, "\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ = 35 

cat("MVUE of μ:", mu_hat, "cases per region\n")

MVUE of μ: 4.375 cases per region

cat("Improved estimate of P(no cases):", round(prob_zero_hat, 4))

Improved estimate of P(no cases): 0.0093

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 2: Drug Response Proportion
Scenario: In a clinical trial, we observe patient responses to treatment.
Let \(X_i \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p)\) where \(p\) = response rate.

# 50 patients: 1 = responded, 0 = no response
set.seed(111)
responses <- rbinom(50, 1, prob = 0.7)

# Sufficient statistic
T_sum <- sum(responses)

# MVUE of p (sample proportion)
p_hat <- mean(responses)

# 95% CI for p (using normal approximation)
se <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / length(responses))
ci <- p_hat + c(-1.96, 1.96) * se

cat("Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ =", T_sum, "responders\n")

Sufficient statistic T = Σxᵢ = 40 responders

cat("MVUE of p:", p_hat, "\n")

MVUE of p: 0.8 

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci[1], 3), ",", round(ci[2], 3), ")")

95% CI: ( 0.689 , 0.911 )

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Application 3: Survival Time Analysis
Scenario: Patient survival times follow Exponential\((\lambda)\).

# Survival times (months) for 20 patients
survival_times <- c(14.2, 8.5, 23.1, 11.7, 19.8, 6.3, 15.4, 12.9, 
                    25.6, 9.1, 18.3, 7.8, 21.4, 13.2, 16.7, 10.5,
                    22.8, 8.9, 17.6, 11.3)

n <- length(survival_times)
T_sum <- sum(survival_times)

# MLE/MVUE of λ
lambda_hat <- 1 / mean(survival_times)

# MVUE of median survival time (= log(2)/λ)
median_hat <- log(2) * mean(survival_times)

# MVUE of 1-year survival probability P(X > 12) = e^(-12λ)
surv_12 <- exp(-12 * lambda_hat)

cat("Sufficient statistic T =", round(T_sum, 1), "months\n")

Sufficient statistic T = 295.1 months

cat("MVUE of λ:", round(lambda_hat, 4), "per month\n")

MVUE of λ: 0.0678 per month

cat("Estimated median survival:", round(median_hat, 1), "months\n")

Estimated median survival: 10.2 months

cat("Estimated P(survive > 12 months):", round(surv_12, 3))

Estimated P(survive > 12 months): 0.443

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Lesson 5 Summary: Key Concepts
1. Sufficiency

A statistic \(T\) is sufficient if it captures all information about \(\theta\)
Formal criterion: conditional distribution of data given \(T\) doesn’t depend on \(\theta\)


2. Neyman Factorization Theorem

\(f(\mathbf{x}; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(\mathbf{x})\)
Practical tool for identifying sufficient statistics



3. Rao-Blackwell Theorem

Conditioning on sufficient statistics improves estimators
Any estimator not based on sufficient statistics is suboptimal



4. Completeness

Combined with sufficiency, guarantees unique MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

text:

(Devore 7.47) For Bernoulli\((p)\) data, we want to estimate \(p(1-p)\). Start with \(U = I(X_1 = 1, X_2 = 0)\) (indicator that first succeeds, second fails). Find the improved estimator \(U^* = E(U|T)\) where \(T = \sum X_i\).
(Devore 7.48) In Example 7.30, we started with \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) to estimate \(e^{-\mu}\) for Poisson data. Now start with \(U = \frac{1}{n}\sum I(X_i = 0)\). Show that the Rao-Blackwell improved estimator is identical to the one in the example.
(Devore 7.49) For Poisson\((\mu)\), both \(\bar{X}\) and \(S^2\) are unbiased for \(\mu\). Consider \(\hat{\mu} = (\bar{X} + S^2)/2\). Which of \(\bar{X}\), \(S^2\), or \(\hat{\mu}\) is the best estimator? Justify using sufficiency.

title: Lesson 5: Sufficient Statistics
text:
Homework: Challenging Problems

(Devore 7.72) The fraction of a bottle filled follows \(f(x; \theta) = \theta x^{\theta-1}\) for \(0 < x < 1\).

Find the method of moments estimator for \(\theta\).
Is this estimator sufficient? If not, find a sufficient statistic and an estimator based on it.

(Devore 7.71) An investigator tests individuals until finding \(r\) with an allergy, where \(P(\text{allergy}) = p\). Let \(Y\) = number tested. Use the definition of sufficiency to show \(Y\) is sufficient for \(p\).
Medical Application: In a vaccine trial, adverse events follow Poisson\((\mu)\) per 1000 vaccinations. With data from \(n = 12\) groups of 1000 people:

Identify the sufficient statistic for \(\mu\)
Find the MVUE for \(\mu\)
Find an improved unbiased estimator for \(P(\text{no adverse events}) = e^{-\mu}\)

Description
Welcome to BSTA 551! In this course we will study the theoretical foundaton of statistical inference which includes estimation and hypothesis testing. This is the official course description:
This course introduces theoretical foundation in Biostatistics. Topics will include distributions of random variables (location-scale families and exponential families), data reduction (sufficiency and completeness of statistics), methods of estimation (method of moment estimators and maximum likelihood estimators), convergence, finite and large sample properties of estimators, interval estimation, hypothesis testing, asymptotic tests (likelihood-ratio tests, score tests, and Wald tests), and statistical simulations to evaluate statistical methods.

Course Learning Objectives
At the end of this course, students should be able to…

Explain the major concepts and theorems in statistical inference.
Connect theoretical concepts to statistical analyses.
Conduct simulations to study and evaluate statistical methods.

Late Work Policy
I encourage you to make your best effort to submit all assignments on time, but I understand circumstances arise that are beyond our control. If you have extenuating circumstances that may jeopardize your ability to do work for several weeks, please contact me. We will come up with a plan to keep you on track in the course and prevent any delay in your education.
For homework, you will have TWO no-questions-asked, 3-day extensions: one for the first assignment part and one for either the solutions or presentation. Please use this wisely! You just need to send me a quick email saying “I am using my no-questions-asked extension for Homework __ assignment/solutions/presentation.”
For homework, I ask you to email me directly about any late submissions. You can explain your circumstances and may ask us for an extension. I am very likely to grant an extension, but I want to emphasize how important it will be to stay on track with your homework! Your group is depending on you, and delaying homework may only add stress on the next homework!
If you have a emergency involving your self, family, pet, friend, classmate, or anything/one deemed important to you, please do not worry about immediately contacting me. We can work something out after your emergency. If I contact you during an emergency, it is only because I am worried, and you do NOT need to respond until you are able. 



Regrade Policy
If you think a question was incorrectly graded, first compare your answer to the answer key. If you believe a re-grade would be appropriate, write an email to me containing the question and a short explanation as to why the question(s) was/were incorrectly graded. Deadline: One week after assignments were returned to class (late requests will not be considered).


Attendance Policy
You are expected to attend class, participate in-class polls, and complete the exit ticket. For students who miss class or need a review, I will make video and audio recordings of lectures available. There are no guarantees against technical or other challenges for the recording availability or quality.
You will need to attend all classes. There are 17 classes total, so you are welcome to watch the recordings or come in-person. While I want attendance to be a flexible thing, I need to set certain requirements around in-person attendance to align with the school’s policy. Attendance is measured through exit tickets that will be due 7 days after each class.
This is meant to keep you on track within the course and prevent a pile up of material. Make sure to complete the exit ticket at the end of class to demonstrate attendance.


Plagiarism and Attribution
Please note that this section is directly sourced from Dr. Nicky Wakim’s Course Policies for BSTA 550 which has itself has been motivated by Dr. Steven Bedrick’s Course Policies and Grading site for BMI 525. (Note that this is a good example of informal attribution of someone else’s work.)
In this class, it is easy to use ChatGPT or other AI tools to solve your homework for you. Many problems follow a basic structure that is especially easy for ChatGPT to solve. In this class, you may use ChatGPT to help with your homework. You may even ask for direct answers. However, there are a few things I do not want you to do:

Do not copy ChatGPT’s answer directly into your homework. Your homework is graded for full credit if you turn it in, in any state, so turning in ChatGPT’s answers is unacceptable. I rather see half-written answers that show what you’re thinking than see a correct answer from ChatGPT.
Do not stop once ChatGPT answered a question. If it gives an explanation, interact with it! Make sure you understand the thought process of ChatGPT. Try writing out the process to help cement it in your head. Check the answer with what we learn in class.
Do not use ChatGPT on our exams! Hence, you need to really understand how to solve these problems even if you use ChatGPT on the homework.

At the end of the day, ChatGPT is a resource that will be available to you in a job and outside of school. Thus, we should use it as a tool in school as well! Let me know if ChatGPT helped you understand something! I would love to incorporate it into future classes!






Important



You can think of this class as assembling a toolbox. When a handyperson starts working for the first time, they need to buy their tools. For their first few jobs, they might need help finding their tools or remembering which tool is best used for what action. Eventually, they get to know their tools well, and using them appropriately becomes second nature.
For now, ChatGPT can help us find and use our tools, but we need to work towards using them as second nature!

title: Homework 1
section: Problem 1: Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean
text:
Problem 1: Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean
Researchers are studying the birth weights of full-term infants at a large hospital. Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n}\) be a random sample of birth weights from a population with mean \(\mu = 3400\) grams and standard deviation \(\sigma = 450\) grams.

Part (a)
For a sample of size \(n = 25\), calculate \(E(\bar{X})\), \(\text{Var}(\bar{X})\), and \(SE(\bar{X})\).
Solution:
Using the properties of the sample mean from a random sample that we explored in class:
\[E(\bar{X}) = \mu = 3400 \text{ grams}\]
\[\text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} = \frac{450^2}{25} = \frac{202500}{25} = 8100 \text{ grams}^2\]
\[SE(\bar{X}) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(\bar{X})} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{450}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{450}{5} = 90 \text{ grams}\]

mu <- 3400
sigma <- 450
n <- 25

E_Xbar <- mu
Var_Xbar <- sigma^2 / n
SE_Xbar <- sigma / sqrt(n)

tibble(
  Quantity = c("$E(\\bar{X})$", "$\\text{Var}(\\bar{X})$", "$SE(\\bar{X})$"),
  Value = c(E_Xbar, Var_Xbar, SE_Xbar),
  Units = c("grams", "grams$^2$", "grams")
) |> knitr::kable(escape = FALSE)




Quantity
Value
Units




\(E(\bar{X})\)
3400
grams


\(\text{Var}(\bar{X})\)
8100
grams\(^2\)


\(SE(\bar{X})\)
90
grams







Part (b)
How large must the sample size \(n\) be so that the standard error of \(\bar{X}\) is at most 50 grams?
Solution:
We need \(SE(\bar{X}) \leq 50\):
\[\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \leq 50\]
\[\sqrt{n} \geq \frac{\sigma}{50} = \frac{450}{50} = 9\]
\[n \geq 81\]

target_SE <- 50
n_required <- (sigma / target_SE)^2
cat("Minimum sample size required:", ceiling(n_required), "\n")

Minimum sample size required: 81 

cat("Verification: SE with n =", ceiling(n_required), "is", sigma/sqrt(ceiling(n_required)), "grams")

Verification: SE with n = 81 is 50 grams


Answer: The sample size must be at least \(n = 81\).


Part (c)
Suppose we define a new statistic \(W = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - 3000)\). Find \(E(W)\) and \(\text{Var}(W)\).
Solution:
First, simplify \(W\):
\[W = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - 3000) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} 3000 = \bar{X} - 3000\]
Now find the expected value:
\[E(W) = E(\bar{X} - 3000) = E(\bar{X}) - 3000 = \mu - 3000\]
For the variance (constants don’t affect variance):
\[\text{Var}(W) = \text{Var}(\bar{X} - 3000) = \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]
Is \(W\) an unbiased estimator of \(\mu - 3000\)?
Yes! Since \(E(W) = \mu - 3000\), the estimator \(W\) is unbiased for \(\mu - 3000\).

# With our parameters:
E_W <- mu - 3000
Var_W <- sigma^2 / n

cat("E(W) = μ - 3000 =", E_W, "grams\n")

E(W) = μ - 3000 = 400 grams

cat("Var(W) = σ²/n =", Var_W, "grams²\n")

Var(W) = σ²/n = 8100 grams²

cat("W is an unbiased estimator of μ - 3000 since E(W) = μ - 3000")

W is an unbiased estimator of μ - 3000 since E(W) = μ - 3000

title: Homework 1
text:
Problem 2: Bias, Variance, and MSE
Let \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) be a random sample from an Exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda > 0\) (so that \(E(X_i) = 1/\lambda\) and \(\text{Var}(X_i) = 1/\lambda^2\)).

Part (a)
Show that \(\hat{\mu} = \bar{X}\) is unbiased for \(\mu = 1/\lambda\) and calculate \(\text{Var}(\hat{\mu})\).
Solution:
Unbiasedness:
\[E(\hat{\mu}) = E(\bar{X}) = E\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i\right) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} E(X_i) = \frac{1}{n} \cdot n \cdot \frac{1}{\lambda} = \frac{1}{\lambda} = \mu\]
Since \(E(\hat{\mu}) = \mu\), the estimator \(\bar{X}\) is unbiased for \(\mu = 1/\lambda\).
Variance:
\[\text{Var}(\hat{\mu}) = \text{Var}(\bar{X}) = \frac{\text{Var}(X_i)}{n} = \frac{1/\lambda^2}{n} = \frac{1}{n\lambda^2}\]


Part (b)
For \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\), given that \(E(1/\bar{X}) = \frac{n\lambda}{n-1}\) for \(n > 1\), calculate the bias and propose an unbiased modification.
Solution:
Bias of \(\hat{\lambda}\):
\[\text{Bias}(\hat{\lambda}) = E(\hat{\lambda}) - \lambda = \frac{n\lambda}{n-1} - \lambda = \frac{n\lambda - (n-1)\lambda}{n-1} = \frac{\lambda}{n-1}\]
The bias is positive, meaning \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\) systematically overestimates \(\lambda\).
Unbiased modification:
To create an unbiased estimator, we need to multiply by a correction factor:
\[\tilde{\lambda} = \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{\bar{X}} = \frac{n-1}{n\bar{X}}\]
Verification:
\[E(\tilde{\lambda}) = \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot E\left(\frac{1}{\bar{X}}\right) = \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{n\lambda}{n-1} = \lambda \checkmark\]


Part (c)
For \(n = 12\) and \(\lambda = 0.5\), calculate the bias and MSE of \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\).
Solution:

n <- 12
lambda <- 0.5

# Bias
bias_lambda_hat <- lambda / (n - 1)
cat("Bias of λ̂ =", bias_lambda_hat, "\n")

Bias of λ̂ = 0.04545455 

# Variance (given formula)
var_lambda_hat <- (n^2 * lambda^2) / ((n - 1)^2 * (n - 2))

cat("Variance of λ̂ =", round(var_lambda_hat, 6), "\n")

Variance of λ̂ = 0.029752 

# MSE = Variance + Bias²
mse_lambda_hat <- var_lambda_hat + bias_lambda_hat^2

cat("MSE of λ̂ =", round(mse_lambda_hat, 6), "\n")

MSE of λ̂ = 0.031818 


Theoretical calculations:
\[\text{Bias}(\hat{\lambda}) = \frac{\lambda}{n-1} = \frac{0.5}{11} = \frac{1}{22} \approx 0.04545\]
\[\text{Var}(\hat{\lambda}) = \frac{n^2\lambda^2}{(n-1)^2(n-2)} = \frac{144 \times 0.25}{121 \times 10} = \frac{36}{1210} \approx 0.02975\]
\[\text{MSE}(\hat{\lambda}) = \text{Var}(\hat{\lambda}) + [\text{Bias}(\hat{\lambda})]^2 = 0.02975 + 0.04545^2 \approx 0.02975 + 0.00207 \approx 0.03182\]


Part (d)
R simulation to verify the results from part (c).
Solution:

set.seed(551)
n_sims <- 10000
n <- 12
lambda <- 0.5

# Simulate
sim_results <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |>
  mutate(
    # Generate n exponential observations for each simulation
    data = map(sim, \(s) rexp(n, rate = lambda)),
    # Calculate sample mean
    xbar = map_dbl(data, mean),
    # Calculate λ̂ = 1/X̄
    lambda_hat = 1 / xbar
  )

# Calculate simulated statistics
sim_mean <- mean(sim_results$lambda_hat)
sim_bias <- sim_mean - lambda
sim_var <- var(sim_results$lambda_hat)
sim_mse <- mean((sim_results$lambda_hat - lambda)^2)

# Theoretical values
theo_bias <- lambda / (n - 1)
theo_var <- (n^2 * lambda^2) / ((n - 1)^2 * (n - 2))
theo_mse <- theo_var + theo_bias^2

# Comparison table
tibble(
  Quantity = c("$E(\\hat{\\lambda})$", "Bias", "Variance", "MSE"),
  Theoretical = c(lambda + theo_bias, theo_bias, theo_var, theo_mse),
  Simulated = c(sim_mean, sim_bias, sim_var, sim_mse)
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 5))) |>

  annotate("text", x = lambda - 0.03, y = 3, 
           label = paste("True~lambda ==", lambda), parse = TRUE,
           color = "darkgreen", hjust = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = sim_mean + 0.03, y = 2.5, 
           label = paste("E(hat(lambda)) %~~%", round(sim_mean, 3)), parse = TRUE,
           color = "darkred", hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    title = expression("Sampling Distribution of"~hat(lambda) == 1/bar(X)),
    subtitle = bquote(n == .(n) ~ ", " ~ lambda == .(lambda) ~ ", 10,000 simulations"),
    x = expression(hat(lambda)),
    y = "Density"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The simulation confirms our theoretical results: \(\hat{\lambda} = 1/\bar{X}\) is biased upward by approximately \(\lambda/(n-1) \approx 0.045\).

title: Homework 1
text:
Problem 3: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
A hospital infection control team wants to estimate the proportion \(p\) of patients who develop hospital-acquired infections.

Standard estimator: \(\hat{p}_1 = \frac{X}{n}\)
“Add-one” estimator: \(\hat{p}_2 = \frac{X + 1}{n + 2}\)


Part (a)
Show that \(\hat{p}_1\) is unbiased for \(p\) and find its variance.
Solution:
Since \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\), we have \(E(X) = np\).
\[E(\hat{p}_1) = E\left(\frac{X}{n}\right) = \frac{E(X)}{n} = \frac{np}{n} = p\]
Since \(E(\hat{p}_1) = p\), the estimator \(\hat{p}_1\) is unbiased.
Variance:
\[\text{Var}(\hat{p}_1) = \text{Var}\left(\frac{X}{n}\right) = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{n^2} = \frac{np(1-p)}{n^2} = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}\]


Part (b)
Calculate \(E(\hat{p}_2)\) and find its bias.
Solution:
\[E(\hat{p}_2) = E\left(\frac{X + 1}{n + 2}\right) = \frac{E(X) + 1}{n + 2} = \frac{np + 1}{n + 2}\]
Bias:
\[\text{Bias}(\hat{p}_2) = E(\hat{p}_2) - p = \frac{np + 1}{n + 2} - p = \frac{np + 1 - p(n + 2)}{n + 2} = \frac{np + 1 - np - 2p}{n + 2} = \frac{1 - 2p}{n + 2}\]
Interpretation:

When \(p < 0.5\): Bias \(= \frac{1-2p}{n+2} > 0\), so \(\hat{p}_2\) overestimates \(p\) (pulls toward 0.5)
When \(p > 0.5\): Bias \(= \frac{1-2p}{n+2} < 0\), so \(\hat{p}_2\) underestimates \(p\) (pulls toward 0.5)
When \(p = 0.5\): Bias \(= 0\)

The add-one estimator shrinks estimates toward 0.5.


Part (c)
For \(n = 40\) and \(p = 0.05\), calculate MSE of both estimators.
Solution:

n <- 40
p <- 0.05

# Standard estimator p̂₁ = X/n
var_p1 <- p * (1 - p) / n
mse_p1 <- var_p1  # unbiased, so MSE = Variance

# Add-one estimator p̂₂ = (X+1)/(n+2)
bias_p2 <- (1 - 2*p) / (n + 2)
var_p2 <- n * p * (1 - p) / (n + 2)^2
mse_p2 <- var_p2 + bias_p2^2

tibble(
  Estimator = c("$\\hat{p}_1 = X/n$ (standard)", 
                "$\\hat{p}_2 = (X+1)/(n+2)$ (add-one)"),
  Bias = c(0, bias_p2),
  Variance = c(var_p1, var_p2),
  MSE = c(mse_p1, mse_p2)
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 6))) |>
  knitr::kable(escape = FALSE)




Estimator
Bias
Variance
MSE




\(\hat{p}_1 = X/n\) (standard)
0.000000
0.001188
0.001188


\(\hat{p}_2 = (X+1)/(n+2)\) (add-one)
0.021429
0.001077
0.001536





Comparison:

MSE(\(\hat{p}_1\)) = \(\frac{0.05 \times 0.95}{40} = 0.0011875\)
MSE(\(\hat{p}_2\)) = \(0.001077 + 0.0214^2 \approx 0.001077 + 0.000459 = 0.001536\)

For \(p = 0.05\), the standard estimator \(\hat{p}_1\) is preferred (lower MSE).


Part (d)
Plot comparing MSE across all values of \(p\).
Solution:

n <- 40

mse_comparison <- tibble(p = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(
    # Standard estimator
    mse_p1 = p * (1 - p) / n,
    # Add-one estimator
    bias_p2 = (1 - 2*p) / (n + 2),
    var_p2 = n * p * (1 - p) / (n + 2)^2,
    mse_p2 = var_p2 + bias_p2^2
  )

# Find crossover points
mse_comparison <- mse_comparison |>
  mutate(p2_better = mse_p2 < mse_p1)

crossover_low <- mse_comparison |> filter(p2_better) |> pull(p) |> min()
crossover_high <- mse_comparison |> filter(p2_better) |> pull(p) |> max()

# Plot
mse_comparison |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(mse_p1, mse_p2), names_to = "Estimator", values_to = "MSE") |>
  mutate(Estimator = factor(Estimator, 
                            levels = c("mse_p1", "mse_p2"),
                            labels = c("p1", "p2"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = MSE, color = Estimator)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(crossover_low, crossover_high), linetype = "dashed", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = crossover_low, xmax = crossover_high, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf,
           alpha = 0.1, fill = "green") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.0055, label = "Add-one estimator wins", color = "darkgreen") +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("p1" = "steelblue", "p2" = "darkred"),
    labels = c(
      "p1" = expression(hat(p)[1] == X/n ~ "(standard)"),
      "p2" = expression(hat(p)[2] == (X+1)/(n+2) ~ "(add-one)")
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "MSE Comparison: Standard vs. Add-One Estimator",
    subtitle = bquote(n == 40 ~ ". Add-one wins for" ~ p %in% ~ 
                      "(" * .(round(crossover_low, 2)) * ", " * .(round(crossover_high, 2)) * ")"),
    x = expression("True Proportion (" * p * ")"),
    y = "Mean Squared Error"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")







cat("The add-one estimator outperforms the standard estimator for p ∈ (", 
    round(crossover_low, 2), ",", round(crossover_high, 2), ")\n")

The add-one estimator outperforms the standard estimator for p ∈ ( 0.15 , 0.85 )


Answer: The add-one estimator has lower MSE for \(p\) approximately in the range \((0.10, 0.90)\). For extreme values of \(p\) (near 0 or 1), the standard estimator is preferred.
Additional info: Why does this work? The add-one estimator introduces bias but reduces variance for moderate values of \(p\) and so it has lower MSE. Interestingly, this is actually the posterior mean under a uniform Beta(1,1) prior for a Bayesian analysis. This is equivalent to starting with a “prior belief” of observing 1 success and 1 failure before collecting data, and this “regularization” (shrinkage toward 0.5) prevents extreme estimates (like \(\hat{p} = 0\) or \(\hat{p} = 1\)) that can occur with small samples.
The add-one estimator is a bias-variance tradeoff that pays off when the true proportion is moderate. It’s a form of shrinkage estimation that sacrifices unbiasedness for improved overall accuracy (lower MSE) in the “middle” of the parameter space.

title: Homework 1
text:
Problem 4: Sample Variance Estimators
Consider two estimators for \(\sigma^2\):
\[S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2 \quad \text{and} \quad \tilde{S}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2\]

Part (a)
Find \(E(\tilde{S}^2)\) and calculate its bias.
Solution:
Note that \(\tilde{S}^2 = \frac{n-1}{n} S^2\) since:
\[\tilde{S}^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(X_i - \bar{X})^2 = \frac{n-1}{n} S^2\]
Therefore:
\[E(\tilde{S}^2) = E\left(\frac{n-1}{n} S^2\right) = \frac{n-1}{n} E(S^2) = \frac{n-1}{n} \sigma^2\]
Bias:
\[\text{Bias}(\tilde{S}^2) = E(\tilde{S}^2) - \sigma^2 = \frac{n-1}{n}\sigma^2 - \sigma^2 = \frac{(n-1) - n}{n}\sigma^2 = -\frac{\sigma^2}{n}\]
The bias is negative, meaning \(\tilde{S}^2\) systematically underestimates \(\sigma^2\).


Part (b)
For \(n = 8\) and \(\sigma^2 = 64\), calculate the bias.
Solution:

n <- 8
sigma_sq <- 64

bias_S2_tilde <- -sigma_sq / n
E_S2_tilde <- (n - 1) / n * sigma_sq

cat("E(S̃²) =", E_S2_tilde, "\n")

E(S̃²) = 56 

cat("Bias(S̃²) =", bias_S2_tilde, "\n")

Bias(S̃²) = -8 

cat("Percentage of true variance:", abs(bias_S2_tilde) / sigma_sq * 100, "%\n")

Percentage of true variance: 12.5 %


Answer:

\(E(\tilde{S}^2) = \frac{7}{8} \times 64 = 56\)
Bias\((\tilde{S}^2) = -\frac{64}{8} = -8\)
This bias represents \(\frac{8}{64} \times 100\% = 12.5\%\) of the true variance.



Part (c)
R simulation to verify.
Solution:

set.seed(551)
n_sims <- 10000
n <- 8
sigma <- 8  # so σ² = 64

sim_variance <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = sigma)),
    S2 = map_dbl(data, var),  # Uses n-1 divisor
    S2_tilde = map_dbl(data, \(x) sum((x - mean(x))^2) / n)  # Uses n divisor
  )

# Summary statistics
sim_summary <- tibble(
  Estimator = c("S² (n-1 divisor)", "S̃² (n divisor)"),
  `Theoretical E()` = c(sigma^2, (n-1)/n * sigma^2),
  `Simulated Mean` = c(mean(sim_variance$S2), mean(sim_variance$S2_tilde)),
  `Theoretical Bias` = c(0, -sigma^2/n),
  `Simulated Bias` = c(mean(sim_variance$S2) - sigma^2, mean(sim_variance$S2_tilde) - sigma^2)
)

  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3))) |>

title: Homework 1
text:
Problem 5: Estimating Vaccine Efficacy

Part (a)
In a pilot study, \(n = 60\) vaccinated individuals are tested, and \(X = 51\) show immunity.
Solution:

n <- 60
x <- 51

# Point estimate
p_hat <- x / n

# Estimated standard error
se_hat <- sqrt(p_hat * (1 - p_hat) / n)

cat("Point estimate p̂ =", p_hat, "\n")

Point estimate p̂ = 0.85 

cat("Estimated standard error SE(p̂) =", round(se_hat, 4), "\n")

Estimated standard error SE(p̂) = 0.0461 


Calculations:
\[\hat{p} = \frac{X}{n} = \frac{51}{60} = 0.85\]
\[\widehat{SE}(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.85 \times 0.15}{60}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.1275}{60}} = \sqrt{0.002125} \approx 0.0461\]


Part (b)
If the true efficacy is \(p = 0.80\), calculate the theoretical MSE and SE.
Solution:

p_true <- 0.80
n <- 60

# Since p̂ is unbiased, MSE = Variance
var_p_hat <- p_true * (1 - p_true) / n
mse_p_hat <- var_p_hat  # unbiased
se_p_hat <- sqrt(var_p_hat)

cat("Theoretical Variance =", round(var_p_hat, 6), "\n")

Theoretical Variance = 0.002667 

cat("Theoretical MSE =", round(mse_p_hat, 6), "\n")

Theoretical MSE = 0.002667 

cat("Theoretical SE =", round(se_p_hat, 4), "\n")

Theoretical SE = 0.0516 


Calculations:
\[\text{Var}(\hat{p}) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n} = \frac{0.80 \times 0.20}{60} = \frac{0.16}{60} = 0.002\overline{6}\]
Since \(\hat{p}\) is unbiased: \[\text{MSE}(\hat{p}) = \text{Var}(\hat{p}) = 0.002\overline{6}\]
\[SE(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\text{Var}(\hat{p})} = \sqrt{0.002\overline{6}} \approx 0.0516\]


Part (c)
Find minimum sample size for \(SE \leq 0.04\), assuming \(p \approx 0.85\).
Solution:
We need: \[SE(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \leq 0.04\]
\[\frac{p(1-p)}{n} \leq 0.0016\]
\[n \geq \frac{p(1-p)}{0.0016}\]

p_plan <- 0.85
target_se <- 0.04

n_required <- p_plan * (1 - p_plan) / (target_se^2)

cat("Minimum sample size required:", ceiling(n_required), "\n")

Minimum sample size required: 80 

cat("Verification: SE with n =", ceiling(n_required), "is", 
    round(sqrt(p_plan * (1 - p_plan) / ceiling(n_required)), 4), "\n")

Verification: SE with n = 80 is 0.0399 


Calculation:
\[n \geq \frac{0.85 \times 0.15}{0.04^2} = \frac{0.1275}{0.0016} = 79.6875\]
Answer: The minimum sample size required is \(n = 80\).

title: Homework 1
section: Problem 6: Devore et al. Section 7.1 Exercise 22
text:
Problem 6: Devore et al. Section 7.1 Exercise 22
Consider the adjusted estimator:
\[\hat{P} = \frac{X + \sqrt{n/4}}{n + \sqrt{n}}\]
where \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, p)\).

Part (a)
Determine the MSE of this estimator.
Solution:
Step 1: Find \(E(\hat{P})\)
\[E(\hat{P}) = \frac{E(X) + \sqrt{n/4}}{n + \sqrt{n}} = \frac{np + \frac{\sqrt{n}}{2}}{n + \sqrt{n}}\]
Factor out \(\sqrt{n}\):
\[E(\hat{P}) = \frac{\sqrt{n}\left(\sqrt{n}p + \frac{1}{2}\right)}{\sqrt{n}(\sqrt{n} + 1)} = \frac{\sqrt{n}p + \frac{1}{2}}{\sqrt{n} + 1}\]
Step 2: Find the bias
\[\text{Bias}(\hat{P}) = E(\hat{P}) - p = \frac{\sqrt{n}p + \frac{1}{2}}{\sqrt{n} + 1} - p\]
\[= \frac{\sqrt{n}p + \frac{1}{2} - p(\sqrt{n} + 1)}{\sqrt{n} + 1} = \frac{\sqrt{n}p + \frac{1}{2} - \sqrt{n}p - p}{\sqrt{n} + 1} = \frac{\frac{1}{2} - p}{\sqrt{n} + 1}\]
Step 3: Find the variance
\[\text{Var}(\hat{P}) = \frac{\text{Var}(X)}{(n + \sqrt{n})^2} = \frac{np(1-p)}{n(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2} = \frac{p(1-p)}{(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2}\]
Step 4: Calculate MSE
\[\text{MSE}(\hat{P}) = \text{Var}(\hat{P}) + [\text{Bias}(\hat{P})]^2\]
\[= \frac{p(1-p)}{(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2} + \frac{(\frac{1}{2} - p)^2}{(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2}\]
\[= \frac{p(1-p) + \left(\frac{1}{2} - p\right)^2}{(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2}\]
Expand the numerator: \[p(1-p) + \left(\frac{1}{2} - p\right)^2 = p - p^2 + \frac{1}{4} - p + p^2 = \frac{1}{4}\]
Therefore:
\[\boxed{\text{MSE}(\hat{P}) = \frac{1/4}{(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2} = \frac{1}{4(\sqrt{n} + 1)^2}}\]
What is interesting?
The MSE does not depend on \(p\)! For most proportion estimators, the MSE depends on the unknown value of \(p\). This is another Bayesian-derived estimator (posterior mean under a Beta(\(\sqrt{n}/2\), \(\sqrt{n}/2\))) and it results in MSE across all values of \(p\).


Part (b)
Compare to the usual estimator \(\hat{p} = X/n\).
Solution:
The usual estimator has: \[\text{MSE}(\hat{p}) = \frac{p(1-p)}{n}\]
which depends on \(p\) and is maximized at \(p = 0.5\) where \(\text{MSE}(\hat{p}) = \frac{0.25}{n}\).

n_values <- c(16, 36, 64, 100)

mse_data <- crossing(
  p = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01),
  n = n_values
) |>
  mutate(
    mse_usual = p * (1 - p) / n,
    mse_bayesian = 1 / (4 * (sqrt(n) + 1)^2),
    n_label = paste("n =", n)
  )

mse_data |>
  pivot_longer(cols = c(mse_usual, mse_bayesian), names_to = "Estimator", values_to = "MSE") |>
  mutate(Estimator = ifelse(Estimator == "mse_usual", "Usual (X/n)", "Bayesian-Adjusted")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p, y = MSE, color = Estimator, linetype = Estimator)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~n_label, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("darkred", "steelblue")) +
  labs(
    title = "MSE Comparison: Usual vs. Bayesian-Adjusted Estimator",
    subtitle = "Bayesian estimator has constant MSE (horizontal line)",
    x = "True Proportion (p)",
    y = "Mean Squared Error"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")








Conclusions:

The Bayesian-adjusted estimator has constant MSE regardless of \(p\) (shown as horizontal lines).
The usual estimator has MSE that varies with \(p\), maximized at \(p = 0.5\).
For moderate values of \(p\) (roughly between 0.15 and 0.85 depending on \(n\)), the Bayesian estimator has lower MSE.
For extreme values of \(p\) (near 0 or 1), the usual estimator is preferred.
As \(n\) increases, both MSEs decrease, but the crossover points shift, with the Bayesian estimator winning over a narrower range of \(p\) values.
The constant-MSE property is particularly valuable when we have no prior information about \(p\), as it provides a “minimax” type guarantee.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Review: Where We Left Off
Key concepts from Lessons 1-5:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: Properties for evaluating estimators
MVUE: Minimum variance unbiased estimators
MLE: Maximum likelihood estimation
Sufficient statistics: Data reduction without information loss


Today’s Goals:

Move from point estimates to interval estimates
Understand the concept of confidence level
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Explore the relationship between precision and confidence

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
From Point Estimates to Intervals
A point estimate like \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) tells us nothing about precision or reliability.

Consider: A clinical trial testing a new blood pressure medication

# Blood pressure reductions (mmHg) from 25 patients
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)

cat("Point estimate of mean BP reduction:", round(mean(bp_reductions), 2), "mmHg\n")

Point estimate of mean BP reduction: 11.67 mmHg










The Key Question


How close is \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) mmHg to the true population mean \(\mu\)? Could we get a different answer with different patients?

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Confidence Interval Approach
Instead of a single number, we report an interval of plausible values.

Definition: A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that, with a specified level of confidence, contains the true parameter value.








Two Key Properties of CIs



Confidence level: How reliable is the interval? (e.g., 95%)
Width: How precise is our estimate? (narrower = more precise)






The tradeoff: Higher confidence → Wider interval → Less precision

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Setup: The Idealized Scenario
Assumptions:

\(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) is a random sample from a normal population
The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known


While \(\sigma\) known is unrealistic, this case:

Illustrates the fundamental concepts
Provides the foundation for more realistic scenarios
Is approximately valid when \(n\) is very large

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Starting Point: The Sampling Distribution
From the Central Limit Theorem and properties of normal distributions:
\[\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\]

Standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)\]


This \(Z\) has a known distribution (standard normal) that does not depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Pivotal Quantity






Definition (Devore 8.1)


A pivotal quantity is a random variable \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) such that:

It is a function of both the data and the unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Its probability distribution does not depend on \(\theta\) or any other unknown parameters





Our pivotal quantity:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]

✓ Depends on data (\(\bar{X}\)) and unknown parameter (\(\mu\))
✓ Distribution is \(N(0, 1)\) — doesn’t depend on \(\mu\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 1
For the standard normal distribution, we know:
\[P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95\]



Code
tibble(z = seq(-4, 4, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(z),
         fill_region = ifelse(abs(z) <= 1.96, "Middle 95%", "Tails")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = z, y = density, fill = fill_region)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Middle 95%" = "steelblue", "Tails" = "gray80")) +
  labs(title = "Standard Normal Distribution", 
       subtitle = "P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95",
       x = "Z", y = "Density", fill = "") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.15, label = "0.95", size = 6, color = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 2
Substitute our pivotal quantity:
\[P\left(-1.96 < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.96\right) = 0.95\]

Isolate \(\mu\): Multiply all parts by \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\):
\[P\left(-1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \bar{X} - \mu < 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]


Rearrange (subtract \(\bar{X}\), multiply by \(-1\)):
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Random Interval






Key Insight


The interval \(\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\) is random because \(\bar{X}\) is random.




Before sampling: With probability 0.95, this random interval will contain \(\mu\).
After sampling: We observe \(\bar{x}\) and compute the interval. The interval is now fixed — it either contains \(\mu\) or it doesn’t.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The 95% Confidence Interval






Definition (Devore 8.1)


A 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) (with known \(\sigma\)) is:
\[\left(\bar{x} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{x} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
or equivalently: \(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)




Components:

\(\bar{x}\) = point estimate (center of the interval)
\(1.96 \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = margin of error
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = standard error of \(\bar{X}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Titanium Alloy Tensile Strength (Devore 8.1-8.2)
Problem: An engineer wants to estimate the true mean tensile strength of a titanium alloy weld. Previous tests suggest \(\sigma = 55\) MPa. A sample of \(n = 31\) welds gives \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.

Calculate the 95% CI:

sigma <- 55
n <- 31
xbar <- 1064
z_crit <- 1.96

margin_error <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("95% CI: (", round(lower, 1), ",", round(upper, 1), ") MPa\n")

95% CI: ( 1044.6 , 1083.4 ) MPa

cat("Margin of Error:", round(margin_error, 1), "MPa\n")

Margin of Error: 19.4 MPa




Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Pressure Medication
Scenario: A clinical trial measures systolic BP reduction (mmHg) for a new medication. Assume \(\sigma = 5\) mmHg (from prior studies). With \(n = 25\) patients:

# Data
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)
sigma <- 5
n <- length(bp_reductions)
xbar <- mean(bp_reductions)

# 95% CI
margin_error <- 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n)
ci_lower <- xbar - margin_error
ci_upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar, 2), "mmHg\n")

Sample mean: 11.67 mmHg

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci_lower, 2), ",", round(ci_upper, 2), ") mmHg\n")

95% CI: ( 9.71 , 13.63 ) mmHg



Clinical interpretation: We’re 95% confident the medication reduces systolic BP by between 9.32 and 13.24 mmHg on average.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Does “95% Confident” Mean?






Common Misconception


WRONG: “There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (9.32, 13.24).”




Why is this wrong?

\(\mu\) is a fixed (though unknown) constant
The interval (9.32, 13.24) is fixed after we compute it
There’s no probability involved — \(\mu\) either is or isn’t in this specific interval

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Correct Interpretation






Frequentist Interpretation


If we were to repeat this sampling procedure many times:

Each time computing a 95% CI from a new random sample
95% of those intervals would contain the true \(\mu\)





In other words: The method works 95% of the time, not this specific interval.


Think of it as confidence in the procedure, not in the specific interval.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Simulation: Understanding Confidence Level


Code
set.seed(2024)
mu_true <- 11  # True mean BP reduction
sigma <- 5
n <- 25
n_samples <- 100

# Generate 100 confidence intervals
ci_sim <- tibble(sample_id = 1:n_samples) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(sample_id, ~rnorm(n, mu_true, sigma)),
    xbar = map_dbl(data, mean),
    lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    contains_mu = lower < mu_true & upper > mu_true
  )

coverage <- mean(ci_sim$contains_mu)

# Plot
ci_sim |>
  slice_head(n = 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = sample_id)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sample_id, color = contains_mu),
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar, color = contains_mu), size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_true, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "orange", "TRUE" = "steelblue"),
                     labels = c("Misses μ", "Contains μ")) +
  labs(title = paste0("50 of ", n_samples, " Simulated 95% CIs"),
       subtitle = paste0("Coverage: ", round(100*coverage, 1), "% contain true μ = ", mu_true),
       x = "BP Reduction (mmHg)", y = "Sample Number", color = "") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Insight from Simulation

cat("Out of", n_samples, "intervals:\n")

Out of 100 intervals:

cat("-", sum(ci_sim$contains_mu), "contain the true μ\n")

- 98 contain the true μ

cat("-", sum(!ci_sim$contains_mu), "miss the true μ\n")

- 2 miss the true μ

cat("\nEmpirical coverage:", round(100*coverage, 1), "%\n")


Empirical coverage: 98 %

cat("Expected coverage: 95%\n")

Expected coverage: 95%









Practical Interpretation


When we report a 95% CI, we’re using a reliable method. About 1 in 20 times, we’ll be unlucky and our interval won’t contain the true value — but we won’t know which times those are!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
General Confidence Interval Formula
To construct a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI, we use \(z_{\alpha/2}\) — the critical value that captures upper tail area \(\alpha/2\).







General CI for \(\mu\) (Known \(\sigma\))


\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\) for \(Z \sim N(0,1)\).

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: The Width of a Confidence Interval
text:
The Width of a Confidence Interval
The width of a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI is:
\[w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Width depends on:







Factor
Effect on Width




\(\uparrow\) Confidence level
Width increases (larger \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\uparrow\) Sample size \(n\)
Width decreases (larger \(\sqrt{n}\))


\(\uparrow\) Population SD \(\sigma\)
Width increases

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
The question: How large a sample do we need to achieve a desired width \(w\) at a specified confidence level?

From \(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), solving for \(n\):






Sample Size Formula (Devore 8.6)


\[n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w/2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w}\right)^2\]
where \(w/2\) is the desired margin of error.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Response Time Study (Devore 8.4)
Problem: A new operating system is installed. Response time is normally distributed with \(\sigma = 25\) ms. What sample size ensures a 95% CI with width at most 10 ms?


sigma <- 25
w <- 10  # desired width
z_crit <- 1.96

n_required <- (2 * z_crit * sigma / w)^2
cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "\n")

Required sample size: 97 




Check:

n <- 97
actual_width <- 2 * z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Actual width with n =", n, ":", round(actual_width, 2), "ms\n")

Actual width with n = 97 : 9.95 ms

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
text:
Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
Scenario: Planning a trial for a hypertension drug. Prior studies suggest \(\sigma = 8\) mmHg for BP reduction. You want to estimate the true mean reduction to within 2 mmHg with 99% confidence.

sigma <- 8
margin_error <- 2  # desired margin of error
z_crit <- 2.576  # for 99% CI

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:\n")

For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 107 patients



What if we use 95% confidence instead?

z_crit_95 <- 1.96
n_required_95 <- (z_crit_95 * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("\nFor 95% CI with same margin of error:\n")


For 95% CI with same margin of error:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 62 patients

cat("Savings:", ceiling(n_required) - ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Savings: 45 patients

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size vs. Precision


Code
# Show how sample size affects width
sample_sizes <- seq(10, 200, 5)
sigma <- 25

width_data <- tibble(n = sample_sizes) |>
  mutate(
    width_90 = 2 * 1.645 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_95 = 2 * 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_99 = 2 * 2.576 * sigma / sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("width"), names_to = "conf_level", values_to = "width") |>
  mutate(conf_level = case_when(
    conf_level == "width_90" ~ "90%",
    conf_level == "width_95" ~ "95%",
    conf_level == "width_99" ~ "99%"
  ))

ggplot(width_data, aes(x = n, y = width, color = conf_level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  annotate("text", x = 180, y = 11, label = "Target width = 10", size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("90%" = "darkblue", "95%" = "steelblue", "99%" = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "CI Width vs. Sample Size",
       subtitle = "σ = 25, showing diminishing returns",
       x = "Sample Size (n)", y = "CI Width", color = "Confidence\nLevel") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only need a lower bound or upper bound for the parameter.

Examples:

A surgeon wants only a lower bound for average remission time after cancer surgery
A manufacturer wants only an upper bound for average defect rate
An engineer wants only a lower bound for mean tensile strength

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Derivation of One-Sided Bounds
For a 95% lower confidence bound:
\[P(Z < 1.645) = 0.95\]
\[P\left(\frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.645\right) = 0.95\]

Rearranging:
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\right) = 0.95\]






One-Sided Confidence Bounds



95% Lower Bound: \(\bar{x} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
95% Upper Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Tensile Strength Lower Bound (Devore 8.7)
Problem: For the titanium alloy weld data (\(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa, \(n = 31\)), compute a 95% lower confidence bound.

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
z_crit <- 1.645  # for one-sided 95%

lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("95% Lower Confidence Bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "MPa\n")

95% Lower Confidence Bound: 1047.75 MPa



Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is at least 1047.75 MPa.


Compare with two-sided 95% CI: (1044.6, 1083.4) — the lower bound is higher than the two-sided lower limit!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Comparing One-Sided and Two-Sided Intervals


Code
# Visual comparison - draw each interval type separately
ggplot() +
  # Two-sided CI (no arrow)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1044.6, xend = 1083.4, y = "Two-sided 95% CI", yend = "Two-sided 95% CI"),
               linewidth = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  # One-sided lower bound (arrow pointing right to infinity)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1047.75, xend = 1110, y = "One-sided 95% LB", yend = "One-sided 95% LB"),
               linewidth = 3, color = "steelblue",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "last")) +
  # One-sided upper bound (arrow pointing left to negative infinity)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1020, xend = 1080.25, y = "One-sided 95% UB", yend = "One-sided 95% UB"),
               linewidth = 3, color = "steelblue",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first")) +
  # Point estimates

  geom_point(aes(x = 1064, y = "Two-sided 95% CI"), size = 4, color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1064, y = "One-sided 95% LB"), size = 4, color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1064, y = "One-sided 95% UB"), size = 4, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Comparison of Two-Sided CI vs One-Sided Bounds",
       subtitle = "Arrows indicate interval extends to ±∞",
       x = "Tensile Strength (MPa)", y = "") +
  xlim(1020, 1110) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12))

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Understanding CI Coverage Through Simulation
Let’s simulate many samples and examine how often CIs capture the true parameter.


Code
set.seed(551)
mu_true <- 100
sigma <- 15
n_values <- c(10, 25, 50, 100)
n_sims <- 1000

# Function to compute CI and check coverage
simulate_coverage <- function(n, mu, sigma, n_sims) {
  tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |>
    mutate(
      xbar = map_dbl(sim, ~mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma))),
      lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      contains_mu = lower < mu & upper > mu
    )
}

coverage_results <- tibble(n = n_values) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(n, ~simulate_coverage(.x, mu_true, sigma, n_sims)),
    coverage = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$contains_mu)),
    avg_width = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$upper - .x$lower))
  )

coverage_results |>
  select(n, coverage, avg_width) |>
  mutate(coverage = paste0(round(100*coverage, 1), "%"),
         avg_width = round(avg_width, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sample Size", "Coverage", "Average Width"))

  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sim, color = contains_mu),
               linewidth = 0.6) +

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Observations






What the Simulation Shows



Coverage is approximately 95% regardless of sample size (when assumptions hold)
Width decreases with sample size — larger samples give more precise estimates
Width decreases proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — need to quadruple \(n\) to halve the width
Intervals are centered at \(\bar{x}\), which varies from sample to sample

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 6: Key Takeaways
1. Confidence Intervals provide interval estimates

More informative than point estimates alone
Communicate both estimate and precision


2. The pivotal quantity method
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1)\]

Allows derivation of CI formula
Foundation for more complex scenarios



3. The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) (known \(\sigma\)):
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Formulas







Quantity
Formula




95% CI
\(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


General CI
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


CI Width
\(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Sample Size
\(n = \left(\frac{2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{w}\right)^2\)


Lower Bound
\(\bar{x} - z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Upper Bound
\(\bar{x} + z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The Central Problem of Statistical Inference
text:
The Central Problem of Statistical Inference
We observe data \(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) from some distribution with unknown parameter \(\theta\). Usually they are identically and independently distributed (i.i.d.), so they make a “random sample.”
The Question: How do we learn about \(\theta\) from the data?

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The Two Key Questions in Point Estimation
text:
The Two Key Questions in Point Estimation
Question 1: How do we construct estimators?

Method of Moments (MME)
Maximum Likelihood (MLE)


Question 2: How do we evaluate estimators?

Bias (accuracy)
Variance (precision)
Mean Squared Error (overall quality)
Efficiency (comparison to optimal)



Question 3: How do we find the best estimator?

MVUE: Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimator
Sufficient statistics: Data reduction without information loss

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The Fundamental Tradeoff: Bias vs. Variance
text:
The Fundamental Tradeoff: Bias vs. Variance






Key Definitions



Bias: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\) (systematic error)
Variance: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = E[(\hat{\theta} - E(\hat{\theta}))^2]\) (random error)
MSE: \(\text{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = E[(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2] = \text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) + \text{Bias}^2\)





The key insight: MSE = Variance + Bias²
This means a biased estimator can be better than an unbiased one if its variance is low enough!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text: Visual Intuition: Bias and Variance

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Medical Example: Estimating Treatment Effect
Scenario: Estimating the true cure rate \(p\) of a new cancer treatment.
Two estimators:

Standard: \(\hat{p}_1 = X/n\) (sample proportion, unbiased)
Add-Two: \(\hat{p}_2 = (X + 2)/(n + 4)\) (biased toward 0.5)








Understanding the “Add-Two” Estimator: The Intuition


What does it do? It acts like you observed 2 extra successes and 2 extra failures before seeing the data.
\[\hat{p}_2 = \frac{X + 2}{n + 4} = \frac{\text{successes} + 2}{\text{trials} + 4}\]
Why +2 in numerator and +4 in denominator?

Adding 2 successes and 2 failures = adding 4 total “pseudo-observations”
This “pulls” the estimate toward \(2/4 = 0.5\) (the middle)
The pull is stronger when \(n\) is small, weaker when \(n\) is large

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: What Properties Do We Want in an Estimator?
text:
What Properties Do We Want in an Estimator?








Property
Definition
Why It Matters




Unbiased
\(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\)
No systematic error


Low Variance
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\theta})\) small
Precise estimates


Consistent
\(\hat{\theta} \xrightarrow{P} \theta\)
Works with enough data


Efficient
Achieves CRLB
Best among unbiased










The Hierarchy of Goals



Consistency is the bare minimum
Unbiasedness is nice but not essential as long as bias shrinks as \(n\to\infty\)
Efficiency (low variance) is what really matters for precision

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Two Systematic Methods: MME and MLE
text:
Two Systematic Methods: MME and MLE
Method of Moments (MME):

Match population moments to sample moments
Simple algebra, often intuitive
Not always optimal


Maximum Likelihood (MLE):

Find \(\theta\) that maximizes \(P(\text{data} | \theta)\)
More complex, but has optimal properties
Asymptotically efficient, unbiased, Normally distributed!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The MME Recipe






Method of Moments: The Algorithm



Express the first \(k\) population moments as functions of \(\theta\): \(E(X), E(X^2), \ldots\)
Set each equal to its sample counterpart: \(\bar{X}, \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2, \ldots\)
Solve for \(\theta\)





Example: Exponential(\(\lambda\))

Population moment: \(E(X) = 1/\lambda\)
Set equal: \(1/\lambda = \bar{X}\)
Solve: \(\hat{\lambda}_{MME} = 1/\bar{X}\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The MLE Recipe






Maximum Likelihood: The Algorithm



Write the likelihood: \(L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)\)
Take the log: \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln f(x_i; \theta)\)
Differentiate and set to zero: \(\ell'(\theta) = 0\)
Solve for \(\hat{\theta}\)





Intuition: The MLE asks “What parameter value makes our observed data most probable?”

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Visual Intuition: What Does the MLE Do?
text:
Visual Intuition: What Does the MLE Do?

The MLE finds where the likelihood is highest — the most “likely” parameter value.

Key Insight
