title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: MLE Properties: Why It’s Often the Best Choice
text:
MLE Properties: Why It’s Often the Best Choice






Three Key Properties of MLEs (Devore 7.2)



Invariance: If \(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat{\theta})\) is the MLE of \(g(\theta)\)
Consistency: \(\hat{\theta}_{MLE} \xrightarrow{P} \theta\) as \(n \to \infty\)
Asymptotic Efficiency: For large \(n\), \(\hat{\theta}_{MLE} \dot\sim N\left(\theta, \frac{1}{nI(\theta)}\right)\)





In plain English:

You can transform MLEs freely (invariance)
MLEs “work” given enough data (consistency)
MLEs are approximately the best for large samples (efficiency)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Consistency: What Does It Really Mean?
text:
Consistency: What Does It Really Mean?






Definition: Consistency (Devore 7.1, Chihara 6.3.4)


An estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is consistent if: \[P(|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta| < \epsilon) \to 1 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
for any \(\epsilon > 0\), no matter how small.




Intuition: With enough data, your estimate will be arbitrarily close to the truth.
Alternative criterion: \(\text{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_n) \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\)


This requires:

Variance \(\to 0\) (estimates get more precise)
Bias \(\to 0\) (estimates get more accurate)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Visualizing Consistency

As \(n\) increases, the distribution “shrinks” around the truth!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The MVUE: Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimator
text:
The MVUE: Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimator






Definition (Devore 7.1)


The MVUE of \(\theta\) is the estimator that:

Is unbiased: \(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\)
Has smaller variance than any other unbiased estimator





Why not just minimize MSE?

MSE depends on the true \(\theta\) (which we don’t know!)
A biased estimator might be better at some \(\theta\) values, worse at others
MVUE provides a clean, universal optimality criterion

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB)






Theorem: CRLB (Devore 7.4)


For any unbiased estimator \(T\) of \(\theta\): \[\text{Var}(T) \geq \frac{1}{nI(\theta)}\]
where \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher Information: \[I(\theta) = E\left[-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln f(X; \theta)\right]\]




Interpretation:

The CRLB is a floor — no unbiased estimator can do better
If an estimator achieves the CRLB, it’s the MVUE
Fisher Information measures the “curvature” of the log-likelihood

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Fisher Information: The Intuition
Key Insight: Fisher Information measures how much the log-likelihood changes as \(\theta\) changes.

High Fisher Information:

Sharp, peaked likelihood → easy to pinpoint \(\theta\)
Small variance possible

Low Fisher Information:

Flat likelihood → hard to distinguish \(\theta\) values
Large variance unavoidable

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Efficiency: How Close to Optimal?






Definition: Efficiency


An unbiased estimator \(T\) is efficient if: \[\text{Var}(T) = \frac{1}{nI(\theta)} = \text{CRLB}\]
More generally, the efficiency of \(T\) is: \[\text{Efficiency}(T) = \frac{\text{CRLB}}{\text{Var}(T)} \leq 1\]




Example: Sample median for normal data

Variance ≈ \(1.57 \cdot \sigma^2/n\)
CRLB = \(\sigma^2/n\)
Efficiency = \(1/1.57 \approx 0.64\) (64% efficient)

Note on Exponential(\(\lambda\)): Why No Efficient Unbiased Estimator Exists


For the exponential distribution with rate parameter \(\lambda\):

MLE: \(\hat{\lambda}_{MLE} = 1/\bar{X}\) is biased — \(E(1/\bar{X}) = \frac{n\lambda}{n-1} \neq \lambda\)
MVUE: The bias-corrected estimator \(\hat{\lambda}_{MVUE} = \frac{n-1}{\sum X_i} = \frac{n-1}{n} \cdot \frac{1}{\bar{X}}\)
Variance of MVUE: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\lambda}_{MVUE}) = \frac{\lambda^2}{n-2}\) (for \(n > 2\))
CRLB: \(\frac{\lambda^2}{n}\)

Since \(\frac{\lambda^2}{n-2} > \frac{\lambda^2}{n}\), the MVUE does not achieve the CRLB. No unbiased estimator can!
Alternatively: For the mean parameter \(\mu = 1/\lambda\), the sample mean \(\bar{X}\) is the efficient MVUE.











Note on Uniform[0, \(\theta\)]


For Uniform[0, \(\theta\)], the CRLB doesn’t apply (support depends on \(\theta\)), yet efficient estimation is still possible via \(\frac{n+1}{n}\max(X_i)\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Why Sufficiency Matters: The Central Concept
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters: The Central Concept
Students often ask: “Why do we need sufficient statistics?”

Answer: Sufficient statistics answer a fundamental question:

What is the minimum amount of information we need to keep from our data to estimate \(\theta\)?



If a statistic \(T\) is sufficient, then:

We can throw away the raw data and just keep \(T\)
We lose no information about \(\theta\)
All optimal estimators will be functions of \(T\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Really Mean?
Scenario: You observe \(n\) coin flips and want to estimate \(p\) (probability of heads).

Raw data: H, T, H, H, T, H, T, T, H, H (10 flips)
Summary: 6 heads out of 10


Question: Does knowing the exact sequence (HTHHTHTTHH) tell you more about \(p\) than just knowing “6 out of 10”?


Answer: No! The total number of heads captures all the information about \(p\).
This is why \(T = \sum X_i\) is sufficient for \(p\) in the Bernoulli model.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)


A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if:
\[P(X_1 = x_1, \ldots, X_n = x_n \mid T = t) \text{ does not depend on } \theta\]




In words: Given the value of \(T\), the conditional distribution of the data doesn’t involve \(\theta\).
Intuition: Once you know \(T\), learning the raw data tells you nothing new about \(\theta\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Neyman Factorization Theorem
Computing conditional distributions is hard. The factorization theorem gives us a shortcut!






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)


\(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if and only if the joint pdf/pmf can be written as: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) involves \(\theta\) and depends on data only through \(T\)
\(h\) depends on data but not on \(\theta\)





Strategy: Look for parts involving \(\theta\) and group them with a function of the data.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Example: Finding the Sufficient Statistic for Poisson
text:
Example: Finding the Sufficient Statistic for Poisson
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod x_i!}\]

Factor it: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^T}_{g(T; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(T = \sum x_i\).








Result


\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Example: Uniform[0, θ] — A Surprising Result
text:
Example: Uniform[0, θ] — A Surprising Result
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(0 \leq \min(x_i)) \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)\]

Factor it: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(T; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(\mathbf{x})}\]








Key Result


\(T = \max(X_i)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).
Notice: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient for the uniform distribution!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?

# Two datasets with same mean but different information about θ
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)   # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10)  # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 



Both have \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)

Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses critical information about \(\theta\)!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Why Sufficiency Matters: The Big Picture
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters: The Big Picture






Three Key Connections



MLEs are functions of sufficient statistics

You don’t lose anything by working with \(T\) instead of raw data

MVUEs are functions of sufficient statistics (Rao-Blackwell)

The best unbiased estimator depends only on \(T\)

If \(T\) is complete and sufficient, any unbiased function of \(T\) is the MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

Finding the MVUE becomes much easier!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Rao-Blackwell Theorem: Improving Estimators






Theorem (Rao-Blackwell)


If \(U\) is any unbiased estimator of \(\tau(\theta)\) and \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\), then: \[U^* = E(U \mid T)\]
is also unbiased, and \(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\).




In plain English: Conditioning on a sufficient statistic never hurts and usually helps.
Practical implication: If your estimator doesn’t use all the information in \(T\), you can always improve it!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Medical Example: Rao-Blackwell in Action
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for Poisson(\(\mu\)) data.
Crude estimator: \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) (is the first observation zero?)


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5
n <- 10
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulation
rb_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum
  )

rb_sim |> 
  summarize(
    `True e^(-μ)` = exp(-mu_true),
    `Crude: E[U]` = mean(crude_U),
    `Crude: Var` = var(crude_U),
    `Improved: E[U*]` = mean(improved_U),
    `Improved: Var` = var(improved_U)
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> 
  mutate(value = round(value, 4))


# A tibble: 5 × 2
  name             value
  <chr>            <dbl>
1 True e^(-μ)     0.223 
2 Crude: E[U]     0.214 
3 Crude: Var      0.168 
4 Improved: E[U*] 0.223 
5 Improved: Var   0.0082


The Rao-Blackwell estimator has much lower variance!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text: Visualization: Rao-Blackwell Improvement

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Completeness: The Final Piece






Definition: Complete Statistic


\(T\) is complete if for any function \(g\): \[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]




Intuition: The only unbiased estimator of zero based on \(T\) is the zero function itself.








Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem


If \(T\) is complete and sufficient, and \(h(T)\) is unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(h(T)\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Common Misconceptions to Avoid






Pitfall 1: “Unbiased is always better”


Reality: A biased estimator with low variance can have lower MSE!










Pitfall 2: “MLE = Sufficient Statistic”


Reality: MLE is a function of sufficient statistics, not the sufficient statistic itself.











Pitfall 3: “\(\bar{X}\) is always sufficient”


Reality: \(\bar{X}\) is sufficient for location parameters (normal, exponential) but NOT for scale parameters like in Uniform[0, \(\theta\)].

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key concepts from Lessons 1-5:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: Properties for evaluating estimators
MVUE: Minimum variance unbiased estimators
MLE: Maximum likelihood estimation
Sufficient statistics: Data reduction without information loss

. . .
Today’s Goals:

Move from point estimates to interval estimates
Understand the concept of confidence level
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Explore the relationship between precision and confidence




A point estimate like \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) tells us nothing about precision or reliability.
. . .
Consider: A clinical trial testing a new blood pressure medication

# Blood pressure reductions (mmHg) from 25 patients
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)

cat("Point estimate of mean BP reduction:", round(mean(bp_reductions), 2), "mmHg\n")

Point estimate of mean BP reduction: 11.67 mmHg


. . .






The Key Question



How close is \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) mmHg to the true population mean \(\mu\)? Could we get a different answer with different patients?





Instead of a single number, we report an interval of plausible values.
. . .
Definition: A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that, with a specified level of confidence, contains the true parameter value.
. . .






Two Key Properties of CIs




Confidence level: How reliable is the interval? (e.g., 95%)
Width: How precise is our estimate? (narrower = more precise)



. . .
The tradeoff: Higher confidence → Wider interval → Less precision

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key concepts from Lessons 1-5:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: Properties for evaluating estimators
MVUE: Minimum variance unbiased estimators
MLE: Maximum likelihood estimation
Sufficient statistics: Data reduction without information loss

. . .
Today’s Goals:

Move from point estimates to interval estimates
Understand the concept of confidence level
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Explore the relationship between precision and confidence

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
A point estimate like \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) tells us nothing about precision or reliability.
. . .
Consider: A clinical trial testing a new blood pressure medication

# Blood pressure reductions (mmHg) from 25 patients
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)

cat("Point estimate of mean BP reduction:", round(mean(bp_reductions), 2), "mmHg\n")

Point estimate of mean BP reduction: 11.67 mmHg


. . .






The Key Question



How close is \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) mmHg to the true population mean \(\mu\)? Could we get a different answer with different patients?

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Instead of a single number, we report an interval of plausible values.
. . .
Definition: A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that, with a specified level of confidence, contains the true parameter value.
. . .






Two Key Properties of CIs




Confidence level: How reliable is the interval? (e.g., 95%)
Width: How precise is our estimate? (narrower = more precise)



. . .
The tradeoff: Higher confidence → Wider interval → Less precision

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Setup: The Idealized Scenario
Assumptions:

\(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) is a random sample from a normal population
The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known

. . .
While \(\sigma\) known is unrealistic, this case:

Illustrates the fundamental concepts
Provides the foundation for more realistic scenarios
Is approximately valid when \(n\) is very large

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Starting Point: The Sampling Distribution
From the Central Limit Theorem and properties of normal distributions:
\[\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\]
. . .
Standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)\]
. . .
This \(Z\) has a known distribution (standard normal) that does not depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Pivotal Quantity






Definition (Devore 8.1)



A pivotal quantity is a random variable \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) such that:

It is a function of both the data and the unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Its probability distribution does not depend on \(\theta\) or any other unknown parameters



. . .
Our pivotal quantity:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]

✓ Depends on data (\(\bar{X}\)) and unknown parameter (\(\mu\))
✓ Distribution is \(N(0, 1)\) — doesn’t depend on \(\mu\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 1
For the standard normal distribution, we know:
\[P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95\]
. . .


Code
tibble(z = seq(-4, 4, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(z),
         fill_region = ifelse(abs(z) <= 1.96, "Middle 95%", "Tails")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = z, y = density, fill = fill_region)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Middle 95%" = "steelblue", "Tails" = "gray80")) +
  labs(title = "Standard Normal Distribution", 
       subtitle = "P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95",
       x = "Z", y = "Density", fill = "") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.15, label = "0.95", size = 6, color = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 2
Substitute our pivotal quantity:
\[P\left(-1.96 < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.96\right) = 0.95\]
. . .
Isolate \(\mu\): Multiply all parts by \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\):
\[P\left(-1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \bar{X} - \mu < 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]
. . .
Rearrange (subtract \(\bar{X}\), multiply by \(-1\)):
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Random Interval






Key Insight



The interval \(\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\) is random because \(\bar{X}\) is random.


. . .
Before sampling: With probability 0.95, this random interval will contain \(\mu\).
After sampling: We observe \(\bar{x}\) and compute the interval. The interval is now fixed — it either contains \(\mu\) or it doesn’t.
. . .

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The 95% Confidence Interval






Definition (Devore 8.1)



A 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) (with known \(\sigma\)) is:
\[\left(\bar{x} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{x} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
or equivalently: \(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


. . .
Components:

\(\bar{x}\) = point estimate (center of the interval)
\(1.96 \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = margin of error
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = standard error of \(\bar{X}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Titanium Alloy Tensile Strength (Devore 8.1-8.2)
Problem: An engineer wants to estimate the true mean tensile strength of a titanium alloy weld. Previous tests suggest \(\sigma = 55\) MPa. A sample of \(n = 31\) welds gives \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.
. . .
Calculate the 95% CI:

sigma <- 55
n <- 31
xbar <- 1064
z_crit <- 1.96

margin_error <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("95% CI: (", round(lower, 1), ",", round(upper, 1), ") MPa\n")

95% CI: ( 1044.6 , 1083.4 ) MPa

cat("Margin of Error:", round(margin_error, 1), "MPa\n")

Margin of Error: 19.4 MPa


. . .
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Pressure Medication
Scenario: A clinical trial measures systolic BP reduction (mmHg) for a new medication. Assume \(\sigma = 5\) mmHg (from prior studies). With \(n = 25\) patients:

# Data
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)
sigma <- 5
n <- length(bp_reductions)
xbar <- mean(bp_reductions)

# 95% CI
margin_error <- 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n)
ci_lower <- xbar - margin_error
ci_upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar, 2), "mmHg\n")

Sample mean: 11.67 mmHg

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci_lower, 2), ",", round(ci_upper, 2), ") mmHg\n")

95% CI: ( 9.71 , 13.63 ) mmHg


. . .
Clinical interpretation: We’re 95% confident the medication reduces systolic BP by between 9.32 and 13.24 mmHg on average.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Does “95% Confident” Mean?






Common Misconception



WRONG: “There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (9.32, 13.24).”


. . .
Why is this wrong?

\(\mu\) is a fixed (though unknown) constant
The interval (9.32, 13.24) is fixed after we compute it
There’s no probability involved — \(\mu\) either is or isn’t in this specific interval

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Correct Interpretation






Frequentist Interpretation



If we were to repeat this sampling procedure many times:

Each time computing a 95% CI from a new random sample
95% of those intervals would contain the true \(\mu\)



. . .
In other words: The method works 95% of the time, not this specific interval.
. . .
Think of it as confidence in the procedure, not in the specific interval.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Simulation: Understanding Confidence Level


Code
set.seed(2024)
mu_true <- 11  # True mean BP reduction
sigma <- 5
n <- 25
n_samples <- 100

# Generate 100 confidence intervals
ci_sim <- tibble(sample_id = 1:n_samples) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(sample_id, ~rnorm(n, mu_true, sigma)),
    xbar = map_dbl(data, mean),
    lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    contains_mu = lower < mu_true & upper > mu_true
  )

coverage <- mean(ci_sim$contains_mu)

# Plot
ci_sim |>
  slice_head(n = 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = sample_id)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sample_id, color = contains_mu),
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar, color = contains_mu), size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_true, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "orange", "TRUE" = "steelblue"),
                     labels = c("Misses μ", "Contains μ")) +
  labs(title = paste0("50 of ", n_samples, " Simulated 95% CIs"),
       subtitle = paste0("Coverage: ", round(100*coverage, 1), "% contain true μ = ", mu_true),
       x = "BP Reduction (mmHg)", y = "Sample Number", color = "") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Insight from Simulation

cat("Out of", n_samples, "intervals:\n")

Out of 100 intervals:

cat("-", sum(ci_sim$contains_mu), "contain the true μ\n")

- 98 contain the true μ

cat("-", sum(!ci_sim$contains_mu), "miss the true μ\n")

- 2 miss the true μ

cat("\nEmpirical coverage:", round(100*coverage, 1), "%\n")


Empirical coverage: 98 %

cat("Expected coverage: 95%\n")

Expected coverage: 95%


. . .






Practical Interpretation



When we report a 95% CI, we’re using a reliable method. About 1 in 20 times, we’ll be unlucky and our interval won’t contain the true value — but we won’t know which times those are!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
General Confidence Interval Formula
To construct a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI, we use \(z_{\alpha/2}\) — the critical value that captures upper tail area \(\alpha/2\).
. . .






General CI for \(\mu\) (Known \(\sigma\))



\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\) for \(Z \sim N(0,1)\).


. . .

The Confidence-Precision Tradeoff

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: The Width of a Confidence Interval
text:
The Width of a Confidence Interval
The width of a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI is:
\[w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
. . .
Width depends on:







Factor
Effect on Width




\(\uparrow\) Confidence level
Width increases (larger \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\uparrow\) Sample size \(n\)
Width decreases (larger \(\sqrt{n}\))


\(\uparrow\) Population SD \(\sigma\)
Width increases

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
The question: How large a sample do we need to achieve a desired width \(w\) at a specified confidence level?
. . .
From \(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), solving for \(n\):






Sample Size Formula (Devore 8.6)



\[n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w/2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w}\right)^2\]
where \(w/2\) is the desired margin of error.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Response Time Study (Devore 8.4)
Problem: A new operating system is installed. Response time is normally distributed with \(\sigma = 25\) ms. What sample size ensures a 95% CI with width at most 10 ms?
. . .

sigma <- 25
w <- 10  # desired width
z_crit <- 1.96

n_required <- (2 * z_crit * sigma / w)^2
cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "\n")

Required sample size: 97 


. . .
Check:

n <- 97
actual_width <- 2 * z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Actual width with n =", n, ":", round(actual_width, 2), "ms\n")

Actual width with n = 97 : 9.95 ms

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
text:
Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
Scenario: Planning a trial for a hypertension drug. Prior studies suggest \(\sigma = 8\) mmHg for BP reduction. You want to estimate the true mean reduction to within 2 mmHg with 99% confidence.

sigma <- 8
margin_error <- 2  # desired margin of error
z_crit <- 2.576  # for 99% CI

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:\n")

For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 107 patients


. . .
What if we use 95% confidence instead?

z_crit_95 <- 1.96
n_required_95 <- (z_crit_95 * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("\nFor 95% CI with same margin of error:\n")


For 95% CI with same margin of error:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 62 patients

cat("Savings:", ceiling(n_required) - ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Savings: 45 patients

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size vs. Precision


Code
# Show how sample size affects width
sample_sizes <- seq(10, 200, 5)
sigma <- 25

width_data <- tibble(n = sample_sizes) |>
  mutate(
    width_90 = 2 * 1.645 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_95 = 2 * 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_99 = 2 * 2.576 * sigma / sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("width"), names_to = "conf_level", values_to = "width") |>
  mutate(conf_level = case_when(
    conf_level == "width_90" ~ "90%",
    conf_level == "width_95" ~ "95%",
    conf_level == "width_99" ~ "99%"
  ))

ggplot(width_data, aes(x = n, y = width, color = conf_level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  annotate("text", x = 180, y = 11, label = "Target width = 10", size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("90%" = "darkblue", "95%" = "steelblue", "99%" = "lightblue")) +
  labs(title = "CI Width vs. Sample Size",
       subtitle = "σ = 25, showing diminishing returns",
       x = "Sample Size (n)", y = "CI Width", color = "Confidence\nLevel") +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only need a lower bound or upper bound for the parameter.
. . .
Examples:

A surgeon wants only a lower bound for average remission time after cancer surgery
A manufacturer wants only an upper bound for average defect rate
An engineer wants only a lower bound for mean tensile strength

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Derivation of One-Sided Bounds
For a 95% lower confidence bound:
\[P(Z < 1.645) = 0.95\]
\[P\left(\frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.645\right) = 0.95\]
. . .
Rearranging:
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\right) = 0.95\]






One-Sided Confidence Bounds




95% Lower Bound: \(\bar{x} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
95% Upper Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Tensile Strength Lower Bound (Devore 8.7)
Problem: For the titanium alloy weld data (\(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa, \(n = 31\)), compute a 95% lower confidence bound.

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
z_crit <- 1.645  # for one-sided 95%

lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("95% Lower Confidence Bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "MPa\n")

95% Lower Confidence Bound: 1047.75 MPa


. . .
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is at least 1047.75 MPa.
. . .
Compare with two-sided 95% CI: (1044.6, 1083.4) — the lower bound is higher than the two-sided lower limit!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Comparing One-Sided and Two-Sided Intervals


Code
# Visual comparison - draw each interval type separately
ggplot() +
  # Two-sided CI (no arrow)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1044.6, xend = 1083.4, y = "Two-sided 95% CI", yend = "Two-sided 95% CI"),
               linewidth = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  # One-sided lower bound (arrow pointing right to infinity)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1047.75, xend = 1110, y = "One-sided 95% LB", yend = "One-sided 95% LB"),
               linewidth = 3, color = "steelblue",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "last")) +
  # One-sided upper bound (arrow pointing left to negative infinity)
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1020, xend = 1080.25, y = "One-sided 95% UB", yend = "One-sided 95% UB"),
               linewidth = 3, color = "steelblue",
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.3, "cm"), ends = "first")) +
  # Point estimates

  geom_point(aes(x = 1064, y = "Two-sided 95% CI"), size = 4, color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1064, y = "One-sided 95% LB"), size = 4, color = "red") +
  geom_point(aes(x = 1064, y = "One-sided 95% UB"), size = 4, color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Comparison of Two-Sided CI vs One-Sided Bounds",
       subtitle = "Arrows indicate interval extends to ±∞",
       x = "Tensile Strength (MPa)", y = "") +
  xlim(1020, 1110) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 12))

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Understanding CI Coverage Through Simulation
Let’s simulate many samples and examine how often CIs capture the true parameter.


Code
set.seed(551)
mu_true <- 100
sigma <- 15
n_values <- c(10, 25, 50, 100)
n_sims <- 1000

# Function to compute CI and check coverage
simulate_coverage <- function(n, mu, sigma, n_sims) {
  tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |>
    mutate(
      xbar = map_dbl(sim, ~mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma))),
      lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      contains_mu = lower < mu & upper > mu
    )
}

coverage_results <- tibble(n = n_values) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(n, ~simulate_coverage(.x, mu_true, sigma, n_sims)),
    coverage = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$contains_mu)),
    avg_width = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$upper - .x$lower))
  )

coverage_results |>
  select(n, coverage, avg_width) |>
  mutate(coverage = paste0(round(100*coverage, 1), "%"),
         avg_width = round(avg_width, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sample Size", "Coverage", "Average Width"))

  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sim, color = contains_mu),
               linewidth = 0.6) +

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Observations






What the Simulation Shows




Coverage is approximately 95% regardless of sample size (when assumptions hold)
Width decreases with sample size — larger samples give more precise estimates
Width decreases proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — need to quadruple \(n\) to halve the width
Intervals are centered at \(\bar{x}\), which varies from sample to sample

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 6: Key Takeaways
1. Confidence Intervals provide interval estimates

More informative than point estimates alone
Communicate both estimate and precision

. . .
2. The pivotal quantity method
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1)\]

Allows derivation of CI formula
Foundation for more complex scenarios

. . .
3. The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) (known \(\sigma\)):
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

Key Formulas







Quantity
Formula




95% CI
\(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


General CI
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


CI Width
\(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Sample Size
\(n = \left(\frac{2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{w}\right)^2\)


Lower Bound
\(\bar{x} - z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Upper Bound
\(\bar{x} + z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key concepts from Lessons 1-5:

Point estimation: \(\hat{\theta}\) estimates unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Bias and MSE: Properties for evaluating estimators
MVUE: Minimum variance unbiased estimators
MLE: Maximum likelihood estimation
Sufficient statistics: Data reduction without information loss

. . .
Today’s Goals:

Move from point estimates to interval estimates
Understand the concept of confidence level
Derive confidence intervals using pivotal quantities
Explore the relationship between precision and confidence




A point estimate like \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) tells us nothing about precision or reliability.
. . .
Consider: A clinical trial testing a new blood pressure medication

# Blood pressure reductions (mmHg) from 25 patients
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)

cat("Point estimate of mean BP reduction:", round(mean(bp_reductions), 2), "mmHg\n")

Point estimate of mean BP reduction: 11.67 mmHg


. . .






The Key Question



How close is \(\bar{x} = 11.28\) mmHg to the true population mean \(\mu\)? Could we get a different answer with different patients?





Instead of a single number, we report an interval of plausible values.
. . .
Definition: A confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that, with a specified level of confidence, contains the true parameter value.
. . .






Two Key Properties of CIs




Confidence level: How reliable is the interval? (e.g., 95%)
Width: How precise is our estimate? (narrower = more precise)



. . .
The tradeoff: Higher confidence → Wider interval → Less precision

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Setup: The Idealized Scenario
Assumptions:

\(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n\) is a random sample from a normal population
The population standard deviation \(\sigma\) is known

. . .
While \(\sigma\) known is unrealistic, this case:

Illustrates the fundamental concepts
Provides the foundation for more realistic scenarios
Is approximately valid when \(n\) is very large

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Starting Point: The Sampling Distribution
From the Central Limit Theorem and properties of normal distributions:
\[\bar{X} \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)\]
. . .
Standardizing:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0, 1)\]
. . .
This \(Z\) has a known distribution (standard normal) that does not depend on \(\mu\).

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Pivotal Quantity






Definition (Devore 8.1)



A pivotal quantity is a random variable \(h(X_1, \ldots, X_n; \theta)\) such that:

It is a function of both the data and the unknown parameter \(\theta\)
Its probability distribution does not depend on \(\theta\) or any other unknown parameters



. . .
Our pivotal quantity:
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}\]

✓ Depends on data (\(\bar{X}\)) and unknown parameter (\(\mu\))
✓ Distribution is \(N(0, 1)\) — doesn’t depend on \(\mu\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 1
For the standard normal distribution, we know:
\[P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95\]
. . .


Code
tibble(z = seq(-4, 4, 0.01)) |>
  mutate(density = dnorm(z),
         fill_region = ifelse(abs(z) <= 1.96, "Middle 95%", "Tails")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = z, y = density, fill = fill_region)) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1.96, 1.96), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Middle 95%" = "steelblue", "Tails" = "gray80")) +
  labs(title = "Standard Normal Distribution", 
       subtitle = "P(-1.96 < Z < 1.96) = 0.95",
       x = "Z", y = "Density", fill = "") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 0.15, label = "0.95", size = 6, color = "white") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Building the Interval: Step 2
Substitute our pivotal quantity:
\[P\left(-1.96 < \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.96\right) = 0.95\]
. . .
Isolate \(\mu\): Multiply all parts by \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\):
\[P\left(-1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \bar{X} - \mu < 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]
. . .
Rearrange (subtract \(\bar{X}\), multiply by \(-1\)):
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu < \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) = 0.95\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Random Interval






Key Insight



The interval \(\left(\bar{X} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{X} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\) is random because \(\bar{X}\) is random.


. . .
Before sampling: With probability 0.95, this random interval will contain \(\mu\).
After sampling: We observe \(\bar{x}\) and compute the interval. The interval is now fixed — it either contains \(\mu\) or it doesn’t.
. . .

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The 95% Confidence Interval






Definition (Devore 8.1)



A 95% confidence interval for \(\mu\) (with known \(\sigma\)) is:
\[\left(\bar{x} - 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}, \bar{x} + 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right)\]
or equivalently: \(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


. . .
Components:

\(\bar{x}\) = point estimate (center of the interval)
\(1.96 \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = margin of error
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) = standard error of \(\bar{X}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Titanium Alloy Tensile Strength (Devore 8.1-8.2)
Problem: An engineer wants to estimate the true mean tensile strength of a titanium alloy weld. Previous tests suggest \(\sigma = 55\) MPa. A sample of \(n = 31\) welds gives \(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa.
. . .
Calculate the 95% CI:

sigma <- 55
n <- 31
xbar <- 1064
z_crit <- 1.96

margin_error <- z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("95% CI: (", round(lower, 1), ",", round(upper, 1), ") MPa\n")

95% CI: ( 1044.6 , 1083.4 ) MPa

cat("Margin of Error:", round(margin_error, 1), "MPa\n")

Margin of Error: 19.4 MPa


. . .
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is between 1044.6 and 1083.4 MPa.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Medical Example: Blood Pressure Medication
Scenario: A clinical trial measures systolic BP reduction (mmHg) for a new medication. Assume \(\sigma = 5\) mmHg (from prior studies). With \(n = 25\) patients:

# Data
bp_reductions <- c(12.3, 8.7, 15.2, 10.1, 7.4, 14.8, 11.2, 9.5, 13.1, 16.2,
                   8.1, 12.5, 10.8, 14.3, 11.7, 9.2, 15.0, 13.4, 7.9, 12.1,
                   10.5, 8.3, 14.1, 11.5, 13.8)
sigma <- 5
n <- length(bp_reductions)
xbar <- mean(bp_reductions)

# 95% CI
margin_error <- 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n)
ci_lower <- xbar - margin_error
ci_upper <- xbar + margin_error

cat("Sample mean:", round(xbar, 2), "mmHg\n")

Sample mean: 11.67 mmHg

cat("95% CI: (", round(ci_lower, 2), ",", round(ci_upper, 2), ") mmHg\n")

95% CI: ( 9.71 , 13.63 ) mmHg


. . .
Clinical interpretation: We’re 95% confident the medication reduces systolic BP by between 9.32 and 13.24 mmHg on average.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
What Does “95% Confident” Mean?






Common Misconception



WRONG: “There is a 95% probability that \(\mu\) lies in the interval (9.32, 13.24).”


. . .
Why is this wrong?

\(\mu\) is a fixed (though unknown) constant
The interval (9.32, 13.24) is fixed after we compute it
There’s no probability involved — \(\mu\) either is or isn’t in this specific interval

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
The Correct Interpretation






Frequentist Interpretation



If we were to repeat this sampling procedure many times:

Each time computing a 95% CI from a new random sample
95% of those intervals would contain the true \(\mu\)



. . .
In other words: The method works 95% of the time, not this specific interval.
. . .
Think of it as confidence in the procedure, not in the specific interval.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Simulation: Understanding Confidence Level


Code
set.seed(2024)
mu_true <- 11  # True mean BP reduction
sigma <- 5
n <- 25
n_samples <- 100

# Generate 100 confidence intervals
ci_sim <- tibble(sample_id = 1:n_samples) |>
  mutate(
    data = map(sample_id, ~rnorm(n, mu_true, sigma)),
    xbar = map_dbl(data, mean),
    lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    contains_mu = lower < mu_true & upper > mu_true
  )

coverage <- mean(ci_sim$contains_mu)

# Plot
ci_sim |>
  slice_head(n = 50) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = sample_id)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sample_id, color = contains_mu),
               linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(x = xbar, color = contains_mu), size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mu_true, color = "red", linewidth = 1.2, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("FALSE" = "orange", "TRUE" = "steelblue"),
                     labels = c("Misses μ", "Contains μ")) +
  labs(title = paste0("50 of ", n_samples, " Simulated 95% CIs"),
       subtitle = paste0("Coverage: ", round(100*coverage, 1), "% contain true μ = ", mu_true),
       x = "BP Reduction (mmHg)", y = "Sample Number", color = "") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Insight from Simulation

cat("Out of", n_samples, "intervals:\n")

Out of 100 intervals:

cat("-", sum(ci_sim$contains_mu), "contain the true μ\n")

- 98 contain the true μ

cat("-", sum(!ci_sim$contains_mu), "miss the true μ\n")

- 2 miss the true μ

cat("\nEmpirical coverage:", round(100*coverage, 1), "%\n")


Empirical coverage: 98 %

cat("Expected coverage: 95%\n")

Expected coverage: 95%


. . .






Practical Interpretation



When we report a 95% CI, we’re using a reliable method. About 1 in 20 times, we’ll be unlucky and our interval won’t contain the true value — but we won’t know which times those are!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
General Confidence Interval Formula
To construct a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI, we use \(z_{\alpha/2}\) — the critical value that captures upper tail area \(\alpha/2\).
. . .






General CI for \(\mu\) (Known \(\sigma\))



\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
where \(P(Z > z_{\alpha/2}) = \alpha/2\) for \(Z \sim N(0,1)\).


. . .

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: The Width of a Confidence Interval
text:
The Width of a Confidence Interval
The width of a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI is:
\[w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
. . .
Width depends on:







Factor
Effect on Width




\(\uparrow\) Confidence level
Width increases (larger \(z_{\alpha/2}\))


\(\uparrow\) Sample size \(n\)
Width decreases (larger \(\sqrt{n}\))


\(\uparrow\) Population SD \(\sigma\)
Width increases

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size Determination
The question: How large a sample do we need to achieve a desired width \(w\) at a specified confidence level?
. . .
From \(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\), solving for \(n\):






Sample Size Formula (Devore 8.6)



\[n = \left(\frac{z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w/2}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \sigma}{w}\right)^2\]
where \(w/2\) is the desired margin of error.

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Response Time Study (Devore 8.4)
Problem: A new operating system is installed. Response time is normally distributed with \(\sigma = 25\) ms. What sample size ensures a 95% CI with width at most 10 ms?
. . .

sigma <- 25
w <- 10  # desired width
z_crit <- 1.96

n_required <- (2 * z_crit * sigma / w)^2
cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "\n")

Required sample size: 97 


. . .
Check:

n <- 97
actual_width <- 2 * z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("Actual width with n =", n, ":", round(actual_width, 2), "ms\n")

Actual width with n = 97 : 9.95 ms

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
section: Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
text:
Medical Example: Planning a Clinical Trial
Scenario: Planning a trial for a hypertension drug. Prior studies suggest \(\sigma = 8\) mmHg for BP reduction. You want to estimate the true mean reduction to within 2 mmHg with 99% confidence.

sigma <- 8
margin_error <- 2  # desired margin of error
z_crit <- 2.576  # for 99% CI

n_required <- (z_crit * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:\n")

For 99% CI with margin of error ±2 mmHg:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 107 patients


. . .
What if we use 95% confidence instead?

z_crit_95 <- 1.96
n_required_95 <- (z_crit_95 * sigma / margin_error)^2
cat("\nFor 95% CI with same margin of error:\n")


For 95% CI with same margin of error:

cat("Required sample size:", ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Required sample size: 62 patients

cat("Savings:", ceiling(n_required) - ceiling(n_required_95), "patients\n")

Savings: 45 patients

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Sample Size vs. Precision


Code
# Show how sample size affects width
sample_sizes <- seq(10, 200, 5)
sigma <- 25

width_data <- tibble(n = sample_sizes) |>
  mutate(
    width_90 = 2 * 1.645 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_95 = 2 * 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
    width_99 = 2 * 2.576 * sigma / sqrt(n)
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("width"), names_to = "conf_level", values_to = "width") |>
  mutate(conf_level = case_when(
    conf_level == "width_90" ~ "90%",
    conf_level == "width_95" ~ "95%",
    conf_level == "width_99" ~ "99%"
  ))

ggplot(width_data, aes(x = n, y = width, color = conf_level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 10, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  annotate("text", x = 180, y = 11, label = "Target width = 10", size = 4) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("90%" = "darkblue", "95%" = "steelblue", "99%" = "lightblue")) +

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Confidence Bounds
Sometimes we only need a lower bound or upper bound for the parameter.
. . .
Examples:

A surgeon wants only a lower bound for average remission time after cancer surgery
A manufacturer wants only an upper bound for average defect rate
An engineer wants only a lower bound for mean tensile strength

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Derivation of One-Sided Bounds
For a 95% lower confidence bound:
\[P(Z < 1.645) = 0.95\]
\[P\left(\frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} < 1.645\right) = 0.95\]
. . .
Rearranging:
\[P\left(\bar{X} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\right) = 0.95\]






One-Sided Confidence Bounds




95% Lower Bound: \(\bar{x} - 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} < \mu\)
95% Upper Bound: \(\mu < \bar{x} + 1.645 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Example: Tensile Strength Lower Bound (Devore 8.7)
Problem: For the titanium alloy weld data (\(\bar{x} = 1064\) MPa, \(\sigma = 55\) MPa, \(n = 31\)), compute a 95% lower confidence bound.

xbar <- 1064
sigma <- 55
n <- 31
z_crit <- 1.645  # for one-sided 95%

lower_bound <- xbar - z_crit * sigma / sqrt(n)
cat("95% Lower Confidence Bound:", round(lower_bound, 2), "MPa\n")

95% Lower Confidence Bound: 1047.75 MPa


. . .
Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean tensile strength is at least 1047.75 MPa.
. . .
Compare with two-sided 95% CI: (1044.6, 1083.4) — the lower bound is higher than the two-sided lower limit!

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Comparing One-Sided and Two-Sided Intervals


Code

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Understanding CI Coverage Through Simulation
Let’s simulate many samples and examine how often CIs capture the true parameter.


Code
set.seed(551)
mu_true <- 100
sigma <- 15
n_values <- c(10, 25, 50, 100)
n_sims <- 1000

# Function to compute CI and check coverage
simulate_coverage <- function(n, mu, sigma, n_sims) {
  tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |>
    mutate(
      xbar = map_dbl(sim, ~mean(rnorm(n, mu, sigma))),
      lower = xbar - 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      upper = xbar + 1.96 * sigma / sqrt(n),
      contains_mu = lower < mu & upper > mu
    )
}

coverage_results <- tibble(n = n_values) |>
  mutate(
    results = map(n, ~simulate_coverage(.x, mu_true, sigma, n_sims)),
    coverage = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$contains_mu)),
    avg_width = map_dbl(results, ~mean(.x$upper - .x$lower))
  )

coverage_results |>
  select(n, coverage, avg_width) |>
  mutate(coverage = paste0(round(100*coverage, 1), "%"),
         avg_width = round(avg_width, 2)) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Sample Size", "Coverage", "Average Width"))





Sample Size
Coverage

  geom_segment(aes(x = lower, xend = upper, yend = sim, color = contains_mu),

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Observations






What the Simulation Shows




Coverage is approximately 95% regardless of sample size (when assumptions hold)
Width decreases with sample size — larger samples give more precise estimates
Width decreases proportional to \(1/\sqrt{n}\) — need to quadruple \(n\) to halve the width
Intervals are centered at \(\bar{x}\), which varies from sample to sample

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Lesson 6: Key Takeaways
1. Confidence Intervals provide interval estimates

More informative than point estimates alone
Communicate both estimate and precision

. . .
2. The pivotal quantity method
\[Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1)\]

Allows derivation of CI formula
Foundation for more complex scenarios

. . .
3. The \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) CI for \(\mu\) (known \(\sigma\)):
\[\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]

title: Lesson 6: Confidence Intervals
text:
Key Formulas







Quantity
Formula




95% CI
\(\bar{x} \pm 1.96 \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


General CI
\(\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


CI Width
\(w = 2 \cdot z_{\alpha/2} \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Sample Size
\(n = \left(\frac{2z_{\alpha/2}\sigma}{w}\right)^2\)


Lower Bound
\(\bar{x} - z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)


Upper Bound
\(\bar{x} + z_\alpha \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Why Does the Add-Two Estimator Help?
text:
Why Does the Add-Two Estimator Help?
The Problem with Standard Estimator:

If you observe 0 successes in 10 trials, \(\hat{p}_1 = 0/10 = 0\)
But is the true \(p\) really exactly 0? Probably not!
Small samples give extreme estimates that are likely wrong


How Add-Two Helps:

With 0 successes in 10 trials: \(\hat{p}_2 = (0+2)/(10+4) = 2/14 \approx 0.14\)
This is more “conservative” — it hedges against extreme estimates
Shrinkage toward 0.5 reduces variance at the cost of small bias









Bayesian Connection


The add-two estimator is the posterior mean under a Uniform(0,1) prior on \(p\). It incorporates prior belief that extreme values of \(p\) (near 0 or 1) are less likely.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Comparing the Two Estimators: Simulation
For \(p = 0.2\) (a fairly extreme value), let’s compare the two estimators:


Code
# Compare standard estimator vs. "add-two" estimator
true_p <- 0.2  # True cure rate (rare disease)
n <- 25
n_sims <- 5000

prop_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    x = rbinom(n_sims, size = n, prob = true_p),
    p_standard = x / n,                    # Unbiased
    p_addtwo = (x + 2) / (n + 4)           # Biased toward 0.5
  )

# Compare properties
prop_sim |> 
  summarize(
    `Standard: Mean` = mean(p_standard),
    `Standard: Bias` = mean(p_standard) - true_p,
    `Standard: Variance` = var(p_standard),
    `Standard: MSE` = mean((p_standard - true_p)^2),
    `Add-Two: Mean` = mean(p_addtwo),
    `Add-Two: Bias` = mean(p_addtwo) - true_p,
    `Add-Two: Variance` = var(p_addtwo),
    `Add-Two: MSE` = mean((p_addtwo - true_p)^2)
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> 
  separate(name, into = c("Estimator", "Metric"), sep = ": ") |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = Estimator, values_from = value) |> 
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(., 5)))


# A tibble: 4 × 3
  Metric   Standard `Add-Two`
  <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>
1 Mean      0.199     0.241  
2 Bias     -0.00101   0.0405 
3 Variance  0.0065    0.00483
4 MSE       0.0065    0.00647


At \(p = 0.2\), the MSEs are similar — we’re in the “crossover” region where neither dominates!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: When Does Add-Two Win? MSE Comparison
text:
When Does Add-Two Win? MSE Comparison

Key insight: The add-two estimator wins near \(p = 0.5\) where its bias is small, but loses at extreme \(p\) values where shrinkage toward 0.5 hurts!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The Fundamental Tradeoff: Bias vs. Variance
text:
The Fundamental Tradeoff: Bias vs. Variance






Key Definitions




Bias: \(\text{Bias}(\hat{\theta}) = E(\hat{\theta}) - \theta\) (systematic error)
Variance: \(\text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) = E[(\hat{\theta} - E(\hat{\theta}))^2]\) (random error)
MSE: \(\text{MSE}(\hat{\theta}) = E[(\hat{\theta} - \theta)^2] = \text{Var}(\hat{\theta}) + \text{Bias}^2\)



. . .
The key insight: MSE = Variance + Bias²
This means a biased estimator can be better than an unbiased one if its variance is low enough!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text: Visual Intuition: Bias and Variance

text:
Medical Example: Estimating Treatment Effect
Scenario: Estimating the true cure rate \(p\) of a new cancer treatment.

# Compare standard estimator vs. "add-two" estimator

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: What Properties Do We Want in an Estimator?
text:
What Properties Do We Want in an Estimator?








Property
Definition
Why It Matters




Unbiased
\(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\)
No systematic error


Low Variance
\(\text{Var}(\hat{\theta})\) small
Precise estimates


Consistent
\(\hat{\theta} \xrightarrow{P} \theta\)
Works with enough data


Efficient
Achieves CRLB
Best among unbiased



. . .






The Hierarchy of Goals




Consistency is the bare minimum (sniff test)
Unbiasedness is nice but not essential
Efficiency (low variance) is what really matters for precision

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Two Systematic Methods: MME and MLE
text:
Two Systematic Methods: MME and MLE
Method of Moments (MME):

Match population moments to sample moments
Simple algebra, often intuitive
Not always optimal

. . .
Maximum Likelihood (MLE):

Find \(\theta\) that maximizes \(P(\text{data} | \theta)\)
More complex, but has optimal properties
Asymptotically efficient!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The MME Recipe






Method of Moments: The Algorithm




Express the first \(k\) population moments as functions of \(\theta\): \(E(X), E(X^2), \ldots\)
Set each equal to its sample counterpart: \(\bar{X}, \frac{1}{n}\sum X_i^2, \ldots\)
Solve for \(\theta\)



. . .
Example: Exponential(\(\lambda\))

Population moment: \(E(X) = 1/\lambda\)
Set equal: \(1/\lambda = \bar{X}\)
Solve: \(\hat{\lambda}_{MME} = 1/\bar{X}\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The MLE Recipe






Maximum Likelihood: The Algorithm




Write the likelihood: \(L(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i; \theta)\)
Take the log: \(\ell(\theta) = \sum_{i=1}^n \ln f(x_i; \theta)\)
Differentiate and set to zero: \(\ell'(\theta) = 0\)
Solve for \(\hat{\theta}\)



. . .
Intuition: The MLE asks “What parameter value makes our observed data most probable?”

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Visual Intuition: What Does the MLE Do?
text:
Visual Intuition: What Does the MLE Do?









The MLE finds where the likelihood is highest — the most “likely” parameter value.

Key Insight

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: MLE Properties: Why It’s Often the Best Choice
text:
MLE Properties: Why It’s Often the Best Choice






Three Key Properties of MLEs (Devore 7.2)




Invariance: If \(\hat{\theta}\) is the MLE of \(\theta\), then \(g(\hat{\theta})\) is the MLE of \(g(\theta)\)
Consistency: \(\hat{\theta}_{MLE} \xrightarrow{P} \theta\) as \(n \to \infty\)
Asymptotic Efficiency: For large \(n\), \(\hat{\theta}_{MLE} \dot\sim N\left(\theta, \frac{1}{nI(\theta)}\right)\)



. . .
In plain English:

You can transform MLEs freely (invariance)
MLEs “work” given enough data (consistency)
MLEs are approximately the best for large samples (efficiency)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Consistency: What Does It Really Mean?
text:
Consistency: What Does It Really Mean?






Definition: Consistency (Devore 7.1, Chihara 6.3.4)



An estimator \(\hat{\theta}_n\) is consistent if: \[P(|\hat{\theta}_n - \theta| < \epsilon) \to 1 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty\]
for any \(\epsilon > 0\), no matter how small.


. . .
Intuition: With enough data, your estimate will be arbitrarily close to the truth.
Alternative criterion: \(\text{MSE}(\hat{\theta}_n) \to 0\) as \(n \to \infty\)
. . .
This requires:

Variance \(\to 0\) (estimates get more precise)
Bias \(\to 0\) (estimates get more accurate)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Visualizing Consistency









As \(n\) increases, the distribution “shrinks” around the truth!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: The MVUE: Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimator
text:
The MVUE: Minimum Variance Unbiased Estimator






Definition (Devore 7.1)



The MVUE of \(\theta\) is the estimator that:

Is unbiased: \(E(\hat{\theta}) = \theta\)
Has smaller variance than any other unbiased estimator



. . .
Why not just minimize MSE?

MSE depends on the true \(\theta\) (which we don’t know!)
A biased estimator might be better at some \(\theta\) values, worse at others
MVUE provides a clean, universal optimality criterion

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Cramér-Rao Lower Bound (CRLB)






Theorem: CRLB (Devore 7.4)



For any unbiased estimator \(T\) of \(\theta\): \[\text{Var}(T) \geq \frac{1}{nI(\theta)}\]
where \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher Information: \[I(\theta) = E\left[-\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \theta^2} \ln f(X; \theta)\right]\]


. . .
Interpretation:

The CRLB is a floor — no unbiased estimator can do better
If an estimator achieves the CRLB, it’s the MVUE
Fisher Information measures the “curvature” of the log-likelihood

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Fisher Information: The Intuition
Key Insight: Fisher Information measures how much the log-likelihood changes as \(\theta\) changes.
. . .
High Fisher Information:

Sharp, peaked likelihood → easy to pinpoint \(\theta\)
Small variance possible

Low Fisher Information:

Flat likelihood → hard to distinguish \(\theta\) values
Large variance unavoidable

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Efficiency: How Close to Optimal?






Definition: Efficiency



An unbiased estimator \(T\) is efficient if: \[\text{Var}(T) = \frac{1}{nI(\theta)} = \text{CRLB}\]
More generally, the efficiency of \(T\) is: \[\text{Efficiency}(T) = \frac{\text{CRLB}}{\text{Var}(T)} \leq 1\]


. . .
Example: Sample median for normal data

Variance ≈ \(1.57 \cdot \sigma^2/n\)
CRLB = \(\sigma^2/n\)
Efficiency = \(1/1.57 \approx 0.64\) (64% efficient)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Why Sufficiency Matters: The Central Concept
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters: The Central Concept
Students often ask: “Why do we need sufficient statistics?”
. . .
Answer: Sufficient statistics answer a fundamental question:

What is the minimum amount of information we need to keep from our data to estimate \(\theta\)?

. . .
If a statistic \(T\) is sufficient, then:

We can throw away the raw data and just keep \(T\)
We lose no information about \(\theta\)
All optimal estimators will be functions of \(T\)

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Intuition: What Does “Sufficient” Really Mean?
Scenario: You observe \(n\) coin flips and want to estimate \(p\) (probability of heads).
. . .
Raw data: H, T, H, H, T, H, T, T, H, H (10 flips)
Summary: 6 heads out of 10
. . .
Question: Does knowing the exact sequence (HTHHTHTTHH) tell you more about \(p\) than just knowing “6 out of 10”?
. . .
Answer: No! The total number of heads captures all the information about \(p\).
This is why \(T = \sum X_i\) is sufficient for \(p\) in the Bernoulli model.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Formal Definition of Sufficiency






Definition (Devore 7.3)



A statistic \(T = t(X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if:
\[P(X_1 = x_1, \ldots, X_n = x_n \mid T = t) \text{ does not depend on } \theta\]


. . .
In words: Given the value of \(T\), the conditional distribution of the data doesn’t involve \(\theta\).
Intuition: Once you know \(T\), learning the raw data tells you nothing new about \(\theta\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Neyman Factorization Theorem
Computing conditional distributions is hard. The factorization theorem gives us a shortcut!






Theorem (Neyman-Fisher Factorization)



\(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\) if and only if the joint pdf/pmf can be written as: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = g(T; \theta) \cdot h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)\]
where:

\(g\) involves \(\theta\) and depends on data only through \(T\)
\(h\) depends on data but not on \(\theta\)



. . .
Strategy: Look for parts involving \(\theta\) and group them with a function of the data.

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Example: Finding the Sufficient Statistic for Poisson
text:
Example: Finding the Sufficient Statistic for Poisson
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Poisson}(\mu)\)
Joint pmf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \mu) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{x_i}}{x_i!} = \frac{e^{-n\mu}\mu^{\sum x_i}}{\prod x_i!}\]
. . .
Factor it: \[= \underbrace{e^{-n\mu}\mu^T}_{g(T; \mu)} \cdot \underbrace{\frac{1}{\prod x_i!}}_{h(x_1, \ldots, x_n)}\]
where \(T = \sum x_i\).
. . .






Result



\(T = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i\) is sufficient for \(\mu\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Example: Uniform[0, θ] — A Surprising Result
text:
Example: Uniform[0, θ] — A Surprising Result
Setup: \(X_1, \ldots, X_n \stackrel{iid}{\sim} \text{Uniform}[0, \theta]\)
Joint pdf: \[f(x_1, \ldots, x_n; \theta) = \frac{1}{\theta^n} \cdot I(0 \leq \min(x_i)) \cdot I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)\]
. . .
Factor it: \[= \underbrace{\frac{1}{\theta^n} I(\max(x_i) \leq \theta)}_{g(T; \theta)} \cdot \underbrace{I(\min(x_i) \geq 0)}_{h(\mathbf{x})}\]
. . .






Key Result



\(T = \max(X_i)\) is sufficient for \(\theta\).
Notice: \(\bar{X}\) is NOT sufficient for the uniform distribution!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Why Isn’t \(\bar{X}\) Sufficient for Uniform?

# Two datasets with same mean but different information about θ
data_A <- c(2, 4, 6, 8)   # mean = 5, max = 8
data_B <- c(1, 4, 5, 10)  # mean = 5, max = 10

cat("Dataset A: mean =", mean(data_A), ", max =", max(data_A), "\n")

Dataset A: mean = 5 , max = 8 

cat("Dataset B: mean =", mean(data_B), ", max =", max(data_B), "\n")

Dataset B: mean = 5 , max = 10 


. . .
Both have \(\bar{X} = 5\), but:

Dataset A tells us \(\theta \geq 8\)
Dataset B tells us \(\theta \geq 10\)

Knowing only \(\bar{X}\) loses critical information about \(\theta\)!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
section: Why Sufficiency Matters: The Big Picture
text:
Why Sufficiency Matters: The Big Picture






Three Key Connections




MLEs are functions of sufficient statistics

You don’t lose anything by working with \(T\) instead of raw data

MVUEs are functions of sufficient statistics (Rao-Blackwell)

The best unbiased estimator depends only on \(T\)

If \(T\) is complete and sufficient, any unbiased function of \(T\) is the MVUE (Lehmann-Scheffé)

Finding the MVUE becomes much easier!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
The Rao-Blackwell Theorem: Improving Estimators






Theorem (Rao-Blackwell)



If \(U\) is any unbiased estimator of \(\tau(\theta)\) and \(T\) is sufficient for \(\theta\), then: \[U^* = E(U \mid T)\]
is also unbiased, and \(\text{Var}(U^*) \leq \text{Var}(U)\).


. . .
In plain English: Conditioning on a sufficient statistic never hurts and usually helps.
Practical implication: If your estimator doesn’t use all the information in \(T\), you can always improve it!

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Medical Example: Rao-Blackwell in Action
Problem: Estimate \(e^{-\mu} = P(\text{no defects})\) for Poisson(\(\mu\)) data.
Crude estimator: \(U = I(X_1 = 0)\) (is the first observation zero?)


Code
set.seed(42)
mu_true <- 1.5
n <- 10
n_sims <- 5000

# Simulation
rb_sim <- tibble(sim = 1:n_sims) |> 
  mutate(
    data = map(sim, \(s) rpois(n, mu_true)),
    T_sum = map_dbl(data, sum),
    crude_U = map_dbl(data, \(d) as.numeric(d[1] == 0)),
    improved_U = (1 - 1/n)^T_sum
  )

rb_sim |> 
  summarize(
    `True e^(-μ)` = exp(-mu_true),
    `Crude: E[U]` = mean(crude_U),
    `Crude: Var` = var(crude_U),
    `Improved: E[U*]` = mean(improved_U),
    `Improved: Var` = var(improved_U)
  ) |> 
  pivot_longer(everything()) |> 
  mutate(value = round(value, 4))


# A tibble: 5 × 2
  name             value
  <chr>            <dbl>
1 True e^(-μ)     0.223 
2 Crude: E[U]     0.214 
3 Crude: Var      0.168 
4 Improved: E[U*] 0.223 
5 Improved: Var   0.0082


The Rao-Blackwell estimator has much lower variance!

text: Visualization: Rao-Blackwell Improvement

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Completeness: The Final Piece






Definition: Complete Statistic



\(T\) is complete if for any function \(g\): \[E_\theta[g(T)] = 0 \text{ for all } \theta \implies P_\theta(g(T) = 0) = 1 \text{ for all } \theta\]


. . .
Intuition: The only unbiased estimator of zero based on \(T\) is the zero function itself.
. . .






Lehmann-Scheffé Theorem



If \(T\) is complete and sufficient, and \(h(T)\) is unbiased for \(\tau(\theta)\), then \(h(T)\) is the unique MVUE of \(\tau(\theta)\).

title: BSTA 551: Statistical Inference
text:
Common Misconceptions to Avoid






Pitfall 1: “Unbiased is always better”



Reality: A biased estimator with low variance can have lower MSE!


. . .






Pitfall 2: “MLE = Sufficient Statistic”



Reality: MLE is a function of sufficient statistics, not the sufficient statistic itself.


. . .






Pitfall 3: “\(\bar{X}\) is always sufficient”



Reality: \(\bar{X}\) is sufficient for location parameters (normal, exponential) but NOT for scale parameters like in Uniform[0, \(\theta\)].
